utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to be sure that all the interpretation booths are working properly. Does the Prosecutor's group hear me? The Registrar? My colleagues? We give the floor to you, Mr. Niemann. We are resuming our audience. The floor is yours to introduce the following witness. Will you first inform the Tribunal of the level of protection required by this witness which you have asked from the Tribunal? We are working pursuant to an order which our Chamber has taken and, at the request of the witnesses, it planned for a certain level of protection. The witness we are going to call, can we say that this person is included among the protection measures you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the individual that we are about to call had previously requested protection measures, but now has decided that he will testify without any protective measures being implemented; so, at this time we are not requesting any.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was this person one of those included in our order? You said, yes; could you please give me his name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The witness to be called is Zarko Kojic. He was identified by name in our previous request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Therefore, we must modify the order for a moment. I will confer with my colleagues. Mrs. de Sampayo, the Tribunal has decided to amend its order which it had issued on the witness Kojic in the minutes of this hearing. Would you please indicate that this modification has been made? Thank you. You may now bring in the witness, Mr. Kojic. MR. ZARKO KOJIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would take advantage of these few moments to say that the Tribunal will take a break at 10.15, of course, relating to the declaration of the witness; if the person is just about to finish, we will not interrupt him but, in theory, it should be about 10.15. Mr. Kojic, do you hear me in your own language? Do you hear me in your own language? Do you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is the interpretation going through? Yes, it is. I can hear you as well. We have given a declaration to you which we are going to ask you to read while you are standing, after having said who you are. What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Zarko Kojic, and I solemnly declare I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Kojic, you are now before the international criminal Tribunal. You must express yourself in accordance with the declaration you have just made. We wish to tell you that you should be able to testify in serenity and in a quiet spirit of mind before an international tribunal. The floor is now yours, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, where are you from originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am from Vukovar. I was born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you live in Vukovar all your life until 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where was your home in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the Otokara Kersovanija Street, No. 2, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was your occupation at that time? Were you working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- I had just graduated from high school, from secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an incident that occurred in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that on that occasion there were two -- 12 Croatian policemen who were massacred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like in Vukovar after this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very tense atmosphere, and for about a week we did not have to go to school and also -- and all exits and entrances to the city were blocked, but I only heard about this. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this tension erupted into actual fighting in and around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time, not yet not at that moment yet -- which moment do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point later did fighting erupt in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I find it difficult to understand what you mean by "this", after "this".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the Borovo Selo incident occurred in May, you had indicated that there was a lot of tension in the area, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Later on in the summer did fighting start actually occurring between the Croatians and the JNA in and around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Borovo, they started bombarding or shelling Borovo in July. I was not there that month, but on television I saw pictures of the bombardment. Then later, after July, the attacks began throughout the Vukovar and Borovo area, and that was on 24th August when the start of the shelling was serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the 24th of August, did you join in the defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time yet. I returned from holiday on the 18th of August. I had spent my holidays in Bjelovar with my relatives. On the 18th of August I came back to Vukovar and during these days the situation was still quiet, although Borovo was shelled and some shooting was heard from Borovo, but Vukovar itself was basically quiet. There were occasional shots from small arms fire during the night, but on 24th August the shelling of Vukovar started on a serious scale and the whole area was affected, the whole region was affected. I was at that time in my own house and we lived in the cellar until 15th September. On 15th September Chetniks came to some 100, 150 metres from my house, so my mother and I left our house and we went to Olajnica, to a shelter, an air raid shelter, and then I joined the defenders in the capacity of some kind of a logistics group, that I was involved in the logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the answer that you just gave you indicated that Chetniks came within 100 or 150 metres of your house. Can you explain to the court what you mean by "Chetniks", when you use that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I did not know that they were Chetniks, but I can define the Chetnik and say I saw, I actually saw them and that was on the day that Vukovar fell. These were the people dressed half in army uniforms, half in civilian clothes. There were -- usually they had parts of the JNA uniforms, camouflage uniforms, or ordinary fatigues. Also, they were very dishevelled, unshaven, unclean, and there was a clear difference between them and the soldiers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that when you joined the defence force you became part of a logistical support unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where was your unit located in the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the Olajnica. Olajnica was our base from which we went out to buy food, to acquire food, bring water, to bring wounded people into the city and so on. So that is what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you remain at the same location throughout the battle, at this same base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 15th September until the 18th of November, that is where I spent there. That was the nuclear air raid shelter at Olajnica. That is where we slept and then during the day we went on our assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the 18th of November where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, I still spent the night in the shelter. On the morning of the 19th of November, a woman came with a white flag and said: "Anybody who would like to go to Serbia to meet the JNA should go towards the marketplace from Olajnica, and those who would like to go to Croatia should then proceed to the hospital". So, on this advice, I decided to go to hospital, and quite a number of civilians went towards the marketplace in Serbia while the rest went to the hospital to go to Croatia eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the situation like when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived there, there were many civilians there, many wounded people, women, children and the hospital was overfilled. On the 19th of November the army was already in the hospital, the JNA army was in the hospital already, and they told everybody to proceed to Velepromet. So everybody went for Velepromet, both men and women, and I was considering myself whether to go or not, but since my mother was wounded and was lying in hospital, I decided to stay. Actually, I joined the last group for Velepromet, but then a woman told me I could stay with my mother and that then I would be in the company of -- accompanying the wounded people when they are evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this point in time had the fighting stopped around the area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the battle had you been wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only had yellow boots which were not part of a uniform, but they were the boots which I -- it was a good pair of boots in which I could walk very easily and nicely. That was the only military part. I had some kind of camouflage cap, but this was not part of anybody's uniform, not part of the official Croatian uniform, but was something I bought at the marketplace in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of the battle had you carried a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you bring this weapon with you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see other soldiers at the hospital carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did you spend the night between the 19th and of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the basement of the hospital. I talked to my mother long into the evening. We were trying to decide what to do about our future, where to proceed. Then I talked to other wounded people and civilians and then I slept in a chair as much as I could sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th of November, what happened at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I woke up some JNA officers arrived and they had a list of people, and they called out some names, I cannot tell you how many names, but some seven to eight names they called. These people were taken out. They were both, some of them wounded people, some of them were ordinary civilians, not patients. Later, these officers said that all men over the age of 16 and under the age of 60, and that all wounded patients who could move should leave the hospital, and they declared that those who could move were the people walking on stilts, people with very severe wounds in the stomach and in the lungs and so on, but they were able to walk and they were ordered to leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you also leave the hospital at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I left the hospital then, but I was still on the hospital grounds. I left the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was 18 years, 18 and a half years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened after you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, they said we should stand in two lines. There were quite a number of Chetniks there, army people, and they searched us. The searches were ordered by Major Sjivancanin. I used to know his name and when I saw him I recognised him, and he actually gave orders to Captain Radic who was standing to his left and he addressed him directly, he said: "Captain Radic, search these people". Then Radic took three or four soldiers, pointed his finger at us and they actually began to search us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: They were JNA soldiers that conducted these searches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were regular JNA soldiers, but the Chetniks were around us and they watched the proceedings. Then they took all hard objects, pencils, lighters, cigarette lighters, anything that was solid objects. Then they told us to proceed to the buses lined at the back of the hospital in Gunduliceva Street turning -- turned towards Borovo. The buses then turned around and proceeded towards the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you got on the buses were you under guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a soldier with a Kalashnikov rifle. He was in the bus and there was a driver also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The soldiers that were guarding the buses, these were regular JNA soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were regular JNA soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where exactly did the buses take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was along Gunduliceva Street, then Bozidara Adzije Street, across the bridge to -- we went by the medical centre, turned right into the Josip Kras Street. We followed that street up to the crossing with Ognjen Prica Street. Then at that crossing there was another street called Sajmiste, and we proceeded along the Sajmiste Street towards the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Up to the JNA barracks, did anything happen on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the buses we were seated and the buses parked in the barracks, on the barrack grounds, and the Chetniks began to enter the buses. They boarded the buses. They did not do anything but they provoked us. It was some kind of psychological pressure on us. One of them entered and said: "Don't you worry, I cut only noses and ears". Another one came and asked why did you need all this, what was that for? So they simply circled around us, so to speak, and they walked around the buses. They would put knives between their teeth and said: "Here, I have captured a bus load of the Ustasha". Then they took -- I think that there was some kind of fire fighting equipment, some spades, some pickaxes, and they took -- they broke the handles and with these handles they threatened to beat us. Then some more people came. They heard, there was a grinding machine somewhere; you could hear the grinding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the translation has malfunctioned again.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not have interpretation coming from that booth across there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear French in my headphones. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did these ---- now we do not hear in English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We had lost the English translation. Now we are getting it. (To the witness): Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So then somebody, Captain Radic, came into our bus and other buses. He called five or six names. It is my French again -- I am still getting French in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is happening, Mrs. Sampayo? Can you tell us? Has it picked up again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you go on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Radic came. He called five or six names from my bus and they were taken out into a separate bus and what happened to them later, I have no idea. I heard that they had been taken back to hospital and these people are now free. That is what I heard later. We spent some three hours or longer in the barracks and nothing happened during that time. They did not beat us, but the Chetniks did board the bus, but the guard on the bus did not allow them to do anything, so they just threatened us, threatened with abuse, and they were saying, "What are you doing? What have you done to us? Why was it necessary", and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show you a small portion of video which has been previously been marked as exhibit 23. If we can show that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see anything on my screen because -- OK. The lights are falling on to my screen and I cannot see very much what is happening on the screen. Now is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the individual that is shown in this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the person now behind the helmet, behind the helmet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The individual that is not wearing a hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was Captain Radic. This was Captain Radic, but he was dressed differently when he was in hospital. He had a beret at that time and he had a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is this the same man who had conducted the searches of the men outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Not the same man that read out the names of the people at the JNA barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: OK. Thank you. We can turn off the video at this time. Now you indicated that the buses remained at the barracks for approximately two or three hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three and maybe even longer than that -- three hours at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When the buses did leave where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started, we started -- we left the barracks along the Sajmiste Street towards Negoslavci and we turned left on to a local road, an asphalt road but leading through the fields. So we drove along that road through the fields and we came to a small fork where the street, the road, there was a fork on the road. To our left, there were some buildings, farmhouses and old buildings, but we turned right and after some 50 metres or so, maybe 100 metres, we stopped in front of a hangar. My bus did not stop directly because there were several buses before our bus which stopped at the gate of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know this was Ovcara because that was an agricultural estate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Had you been there before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was the road on which I passed my driver's test, but even earlier, as a young child, we were brought there by our school on school excursions or outings and sometimes I rode my bicycle along the road so I knew it was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that there were other buses in front of you so your bus did not pull up directly in front of the hangar, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see what was happening to the people on the buses ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see very much until I came fairly close, until my bus stopped in front of the hangar door. I was in the back part of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When your bus stopped in front of the hangar, what did you observe happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw through the window that people were being beaten, that their jackets hats, caps, were taken away. They went between two files of people beating them, and I saw large numbers of the Chetniks raging there, so everybody was passing through their ranks before entering the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were they beating the men with, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, two or three of them had some kind of handles. One had an axe handle, but most people had nothing. They only had their fists and they also kicked them with their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you pulled in front of the hangar and you saw what was occurring, what did you think was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was on the bus, I thought everybody would be killed. It looked very bad. The situation seemed very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you did, in fact, get off the bus, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I descended, as I descended, they started beating me and I went through the two files. I had to take off my jacket, give them all my documents. They threw the documents on to a pile in front of the hangar. They also took my money, they beat me, and so I was in -- I was simply in a sweat shirt and I ran quickly into the hangar, but they continued beating me in the hangar with truncheons, with batons, with chains. There was some kind of flexible iron rod, and with that they beat me as well. When they finished, when the next person arrived, they simply put me on the left side of the hangar. There was some straw on the floor. We had to stand there first and then we sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you know many of the men who had been brought there on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew quite a number of them. Many of them I simply knew by meeting them, but I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see anyone being singled out inside the hangar for harsher treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered and when we stood on the straw, the Chetniks came to ask if there were any Albanians among us. So Kemal, I think Kemal Saiti, but his nickname was Kemal, he said yes he was an Albanian, so then three or four Chetniks started beating him, but especially passionate and wild was the person who beat him; there was one person who beat him particularly and jumped upon him as he was lying on the floor, and then he would return, regain consciousness, then that person jumped upon him, hit him with a baton until blood started streaming out of his mouth and lungs and nose. I would say that Kemal died, I am 99 per cent sure that Kemal died on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was anyone else seriously injured or killed as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another person that was beaten very badly was Damjan. He was a large man, and they beat him until he remained lying unconscious on the floor. But I did not see this very well because they broke my glasses as I entered and I could not see very well, but the beating of Kemal happened before my eyes which I could see very well. Then Damjan Kovacic was another person that was badly beaten. I think he was called Kole. His nickname was Kole. He had been wounded, wounded in the lungs. He had shrapnel, grenade shrapnel, in the lungs. So somebody asked him, "And you were part of the Croatian national guards", and said: "Why did you do this? Why did you do that?" Then he started beating him, two people actually beat him, especially his acquaintance, and Damjan also began to spit blood after a few beatings. Blood came through his mouth. His wound probably opened in the lungs and Tomislav Papp that was standing next to him asked the Chetniks to give him some bandages because these people had the first aid bandages. So he asked for a bandage, but they did not give him anything, so he covered his wounds, covered his wounds. In fact, there were documents stating the nature of the wounds, so with this documentation, with the papers, they put it on his chest to stop the bleeding but that did not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that most of these beatings were being done by the men you referred to as Chetniks. Were regular JNA soldiers also participating in the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that file through which we had to pass, there were also some regular soldiers and in the hangar itself there were some regular soldiers and everybody hit somebody, but the main beatings came from the Chetniks. There was an officer, a JNA officer, in the mid middle of the room. He said: "Do not beat them" but, of course, he was not obeyed, and he did not actually do anything to be obeyed. But he was -- it was some kind of farcical attempt at quieting the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Approximately how many men that you have called Chetniks and JNA troops were inside the hangar altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether some 40, I would say. That is my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did any of these men tell you why this was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did these beatings go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they beat somebody at all times. There was always somebody who was being beaten. First of all, everybody was beaten as they entered the hangar. Then later they singled out Kemal, then Damjan, in the other part of the building they beat somebody else, and when the situation calmed down a little, then Sasha Guja came in front of me. That is how I know it. "Guja" is probably not his surname, but probably his nickname, or his stepfather was Guja. I do not know his real surname. So he was my age; we used to be friends, go out together in the evenings and so on, and he was in a JNA uniform but he was not a soldier. He actually said that he was a member of the territorials, and this, in fact, was a name applied to local Chetniks. Anyway, so he asked me: "What are you doing there?" I just shrugged my shoulders. I could not answer that. He asked me: "Did you do any shooting?" I said: "Never". He said: "Did you have any weapons?" I said: "No." "Have you been in uniform?" I said: "No". "Have you been mobilised?" "I have not". It was all negative answers that I gave, so Tomislav Papp, who was some two or three metres away from me, said: "No, no, he was in the air raid shelter at Olajnica". Thus, he confirmed my statement. Then he said, he took me aside by the wall to the left of the hangar, to the left side of the hangar, inside the hangar, he put me on the left side towards, near the door. Vjekoslav Sindilj was also there. He was also brought to this position, to this place. So, that was an attempt to save us. So there was a soldier guarding us with a sniper. So he was two or three steps far from us. Anyway, so he was guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when you were actually taken outside the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so I was sitting there for a while, and then they took me out while the Vjekoslav remained, and so they took me out and Igor Kacic was outside and some more people came later, and the Chetniks came out all the time asking: "Who are these?" Then they said: "Well, they are ours". The Chetniks said that we are theirs and there were attempts to bring us back into the hangar. But then Guja would come and some other people came and said: "Leave them in peace", so we were left there. There were nine of us in front of the hangar. It was already getting dark. It was getting dark probably around 5 o'clock because in November it gets dark fairly early, and there were nine of us standing outside. Then -- let me concentrate -- a man came that was beating Damjan Kovacic. Then he asked for Igor Kacic who was 16 years old, and he said, what was he doing there. Then he was told that we were the kind of group -- that we were the group that would be taken away. But then he returned Damjan back to hangar. In fact, all of us had to go to the hangar again where the list was named in duplicate with our names. They gave the one copy of the list to an army officer who was, I think, a security officer. They called it the state security officer. So, one copy of the list was given to him and the other copy was in the hands of the person accompanying us. So, then Kacic joined us again and then, as I left the hangar, I saw Sinisa Glavesevic surrounded by some officers and Chetniks. They said: "You, the Ustasha journalist, who had been writing against us", so he was being abused and beaten at that time. We left the hangar. Kacic was returned to our group, and we went towards the mini bus that was supposed to take us to Vukovar. As we walked towards the mini bus, there was also Ivan Ajasovic with us walking with a stick. Then Miroljub came who was some kind of territorial defence commander. Miroljub, I do not remember the surname, Vujasinovic, I think. I cannot -- I am not sure about the surname. Anyway, so he took Nejasmic again and said: "He is the secretary of the HDZ. Why should he be released?" So Ivan Ajasovic was taken back to the hangar and seven of us boarded the mini bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to go back a little further now. You indicated that Sinisa Glavasevic was being beaten near the door; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What had been his occupation during the battle? What had he been doing during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war, he was the journalist working for Vukovar radio. This was Croatian radio, Vukovar. He was reporting about the events in Vukovar before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you went back inside to have your names registered and you saw him, did you also see other people still being beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them beating some other people, especially Ivan Zvonimir Plavsic, who said that he had not done anything, that he was an elderly man. They said: "We know you; your son was the commander of a section of the city defences", and so they abused him, beat him, and also they beat some other people, but I could not see much because it was getting dark and I did not have my glasses so I could not see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you were placed in the van with the other men that had been saved, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us first to Velepromet and they took us out of the van, but then they were told that there was not enough room for us there. There was a Chetnik there, Ljubin Milikovic, who simply said: "There is not enough room here for these people". So we boarded the van again and we were taken to Modateks. This is a textile plant. So there were a number of women there from the centre of the city, who had been in the centre of the city during the war. They placed us on a marble slab or table which was actually used in that textile mill for fabric stretching. Anyway, so we were left there to sleep on that big table. Nobody touched us that evening. There were some kind of shoulder pads on which we could sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain there at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent one night and in the morning a JNA officer came. He was a Macedonian. He was wearing a jacket and a beret hat. Then he examined us, questioned us. He asked our names, nationalities, what we were doing. They again shouted abuse at some people. There were also Sladana Korda in uniform. She was born in 1973, so roughly my age, but she was very arrogant. She was standing there, and when the Macedonian, that officer, asked me whether I knew her, I said, yes, of course I knew her from the Three Roses Cafe, because this was the cafe where mostly Serbian youth, Serbian young people, were congregating, but I went to all the cafes, regardless, and I used to see her there. So we said: "Oh, good, since you saw her there, that is good for you".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you released from Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then Miroslav Slavic came to get me and he took me to the Svetozara Markovica Street where I was with some old people; some were the fathers, barons of the Chetniks, some of the parents of the national guardsmen. There were mostly elderly people, one was quite old, and myself. This was a building, this was a building requisitioned by the Chetniks. Mirko Stajic took this building and he said that was his house now, although it was somebody else's before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Vukovar after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to 14th December, but then I was not released; I was in this building. The Chetniks would come every day. They did not beat me, but they questioned me all the time, "Who was in the national guards? Who was in the ZNG organisation?", that is Croatian national guards. So, to tell them something, I told them about the dead people and I mentioned those names. For the rest, I said I did not know. I also told them that I had a hernia, that I was imprisoned and that they should let me know because I have a hernia, and they should let me go to Belgrade to my Godmother and to be operated there. My grandmother, my father's mother, was in the uniform, Serbian uniform, she was very loyal to Serbs, and through her connections she obtained a piece of paper which enabled me to get a pass out of the Vukovar. So, on 14th December I left for Sid to live with her brother, and then my Belgrade Godmother came to fetch me and then I was in Belgrade for a while and through Bosnia later I came back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I want to go back again a little more. During the period of time that you did remain in Vukovar where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Svetozar Markovic 70, No. 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Whose house was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whose it was before the war, but during the war or after the war Miroslav Savic occupied the house, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was your grandmother also staying in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time were you free to move about the city of Vukovar at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion during the period that you were there, though, to see any of the Serbian men who had been present at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miroslav Savic, in fact, was at Ovcara and Goran Mugosa used to come to this building as well who had also been at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this stage I would like to show another portion of the video that we marked as exhibit 23. If you would look at this, Mr. Kojic. We can dim the lights again also, please. Maybe we can back it up just a little bit? Then I want to ask you if you recognise anyone who is in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can stop now. The person with the -- the bearded man, he was at Ovcara and he was the one that beat Kemal, the strong Chetnik. He said that he came from Montenegro and he said, he said, "Come to Montenegro to see what culture is."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is why how I concluded that he was a Montenegrin, but he was at Ovcara. He was one of the most aggressive Chetniks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We can conclude the video at this time. Did you have an opportunity during this time that you had remained in Vukovar to speak with any of these Serbian men about what had happened at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only had an opportunity to talk to Miroslav Savic because at one point I said: "What happened to these people?" and he said: "They are all underground now" or "under the grass", as he put it, which means they are all buried, dead and buried. I also talked to Goran Mugosa. I told him that he had taken my documents, he had taken my money and that he hit me on several occasions, but he said: "No, no, that was just joking; you are lucky to be alive".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Other than the men who left Ovcara in the van with you on the 20th of November, have you even seen any of the other men who were taken out of the hospital by the JNA on that morning? We have lost the translation again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you able to hear it now in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have been told that the French interpreters have not touched any buttons. Mr. Registrar, would you have anything to say? Could I suggest that we take a 10 minute, 15 minute break so that our technicians can do something about these audio/visual problems? Really, it is a bit too much so we will suspend the meeting for 10 to 15 minutes. (10.00 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please bring in the witness. MR. ZARKO KOJIC, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is the equipment working? I would like to know. Looking around the room, I would like to know if everybody can hear me, The Prosecutor, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, can you hear me? My colleagues on the Bench? How about the interpreters? Is everything working for the interpreters? I know it is a difficult situation. Let us all try to work together. Even with the most sophisticated equipment in the world, of course, you can never exclude defects totally. (To the witness): Mr. Kojic, please take a seat. Are you tuned into the right language channel? Can you hear what I am saying to you, Mr. Kojic? Are you getting interpretation into your language? Is that OK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear very well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have taken a short rest now. Do you feel reasonably relaxed now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had a cigarette so I feel better now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one additional question for Mr. Kojic. (To the witness): Mr. Kojic, other than the men who left Ovcara in the van with you on the 20th of November 1991, have you ever seen again any of the other men who had been taken out of the hospital with you that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a boy, a young man, who lives at Zevrin near Bjelovar in Croatia. He had been -- he was in the JNA army and he was in a tank unit, and then in September at Luzac he fled from the army, joined the Croatian forces; first served in the Croatian Police, and then had a position in the Police, I think. Anyway, he was captured, and I am telling you his story now, and when the beating began they said: "Do not beat us, we are JNA soldiers." So, four of them, before they were brought into the hangar, they were taken to Negoslavci. He was then in Belgrade. He was tried, and he spent two years in prison in Valjevo. Now he is back home. I know his name but I do not know the names of the other three young men with him, but he would know these names. His name is Hajro, Hajro Dode, Hajro Dode. He is an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Of the men that remained inside the hangar after you left in the van, have you seen any of them again alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor. Judge Odio Benito, would you like to pose any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Kojic, when you were taken out from the hospital the men who were with you in the bus, were they patients of the hospital or they were soldiers or they were civil people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were wounded people, there were some hospital staff and there were some civilians. I did not notice anybody belonging to the Croatian army. But all these people, all the wounded soldiers, were civilian in civilian clothes and they had no weapons and if there were any other army people on the bus they were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, were they all Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume there must be some Ruthenians, some Hungarians and I would assume also some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You told us that when you went to the hospital your mother was there and she was wounded. When and where was she wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 8th Of November we were called to hospital because they needed blood, to donate blood. We sat into a small car, a Fiat 750. We sat in the car. The driver, Damir Bosnjakovic, myself, my mother was in the back seat and there was another woman, elderly woman, called Subasic and Delfa, another woman; anyway, three women sat in the back. When we left the shelter, air raid shelter, and started driving from Olajnica towards Kidriceva Street and in the direction of the hospital, we were fired on not far from the school, but anyway so the school was on a hill across the river and they shot from that direction. My mother was the only one who was wounded, but she had a bullet in her liver. Anyway, we went to hospital. She was operated but the problem was that nobody could give blood for her transfusion. Because I had given blood a month earlier, I was not allowed to give it again, and the other people were so exhausted and so badly under nourished that they were not allowed to give blood for transfusion. So I stayed in hospital with my mother. The two other women were taken back to the air raid shelter, but there was more shooting and our driver, Damir Bosnjakovic, was wounded with a grenade shrapnel. My mother stayed in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened with your mother after the fall of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She left in the convoy with the wounded people, went to Sremska Mitrovica and then via Bosnia to Croatia. She was in hospital in Jujici and then went to Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How is she now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She has recovered. The liver has recovered, but she has had several operations and six stitches because there was no -- they did not have the X-ray so they wanted to check on her bladder so that they had to check by surgery. She also had some bile problems. So she is not in a bad condition but not in top form either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you were inside the hangar, did you receive any food or water or any kind of support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, no, only beating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Zarko Kojic, I would like you to clarify to me a few things. First, you mentioned that on the morning of the 20th of November somebody ordered that men between the age of 16 and 60 and also the wounded who could walk should leave the hospital. Could you recall who, in particular, gave that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A JNA officer came, I do not know his rank, because I was not in the Yugoslav army so I do not know the ranking markings, but he had a leather bag, shoulder bag, and he was an officer. He was a short man, stout with greying hair, so he might have been 55 years old, roughly. He was very similar, he resembled very much the person in the hangar who ordered the beatings but I cannot confirm that. But, anyway, he said that all men and so on should go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see any of those who went out in this case, did you see them afterwards anywhere, or did they disappear completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw them since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You never saw anybody since then? Next when you went to Negoslavci and Ovcara -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not in Negoslavci, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said you went to Ovcara to the barracks, to the hangar, where the ranks were standing and you could pass through the ranks and they were beaten by iron rods, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mentioned Negoslavci; I only said we went in the direction of Negoslavci, not to Negoslavci. We did not go all the way to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The hangar was in Ovcara, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You went down and had to pass through, as you said, ranks and you were beaten by axes, feet, and iron rods and so on. Was Sjivancanin or Radic around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. I did not see them. They might have been there but I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Inside the hangar where there was also beating, there was no sign of Radic or Sjivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that some people were distinguished from the others and received a more cruel treatment. You mentioned Kemal who was beaten to death, as you said, and Damjan; was it because they belonged to a different -- they were Albanians, you said, was that the only reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Kemal, this was the only reason, yes. I think this was the major reason, I assume, because that was the reason. Damjan was not Albanian, but he was one of the commanders in the National Guards, Croatian National Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So you think there were certain distinctions because people were in the National Guard or had any role in the resistance, would this assumption be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the assumption is right, but there was no real rule. Sometimes people were taken out for reasons which were not clear. When they saw a younger person, then they would say: "Yes, you kill some children", anybody. There was a lot of random; some people were accused of having been snipers. For Damjan, they knew that he was in the National Guards; Kemal stated himself he was an Albanian, so they were badly beaten, but there was indiscriminate beating. Sinisa Glavasevic was beaten because he was a journalist of Croatian radio. Damjan Kovacic was beaten because he was in the National Guards. But again, on the other hand, many people were beaten without any obvious reason and they would simply be beaten badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, but those who were saved were saved for a specific reason, including yourself; what was the reason which made them take some people back, in your opinion, relatives or -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my case I was friend of Guja. Guja could have decided to kill me because I was his friend but he decided to save me. There was another man from Zagreb, a volunteer. He was saved without any reason. He simply asked a soldier: "Please save me", and the soldier saved him. Emil was saved because he was a sanitary officer, so he at one point made some favour to a Serb, helping him to open a cafe and he signed the paper for sanitary conditions. The reasons were all very varied and not easily understood; everything was individual and each case was different and sort of random.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, I think you have been asked many questions; I will not ask you any others. I would like to turn to The Prosecutor and ask for clarification as to the origin of the video that we have been shown, as we were. What is the source, what is the origin, of this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the video that we previously marked as exhibit 23. It is a compilation from various sources, but the vast majority of it, probably 95 per cent, comes from footage that was broadcast on Radio Television Belgrade. So this was generally filmed by cameras that had been sent out from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. So these are Serbian sources then, is that what you are saying, that you are using here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. It was filmed by a Serbian news agency and was broadcast and most of these were recorded by Croatian television and then provided to us at our request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is not a real question, but could we again see the three pictures showing the faces of the three accused? Could we show these pictures to the witness again? I think he recognised one of them, but I would like to see if he recognises the Major. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, these are marked as exhibits 24, 25 and 26. If we could have those, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are the technicians ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. Did you wish to see it on the video or the photographs that had been lifted from the video?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I think I would like, and which would be of interest to the Tribunal, is to know whether the witness does recognise the three accused. I think that he recognised the Captain, but I would like to know whether he recognises the Major; I do not think he could recognise Mr. Mrksic, but I think the Major would be important. I would like to see if he does recognise him and, if he does, because he saw him himself or because he saw the images on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. We will show him the photograph at this time. At this time, your Honour, we will be showing the witness exhibit 25.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you focus it better, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe it has to be set on "computer monitor", your Honour, rather than "video".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I have pressed the "monitor" button but what I am seeing is a photograph -- oh, it is a copy. So there were photographs of the man in the video that we saw. So this is an excerpt from the video. Perhaps if we lighten the screen? Does the witness see anything? (To the witness): Mr. Kojic, do you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. This is Major Sjivancanin. I saw him in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have the impression that he was the one who was directing the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Perhaps then, under these circumstances, it is not necessary to extend the hearing, which has already been long, unless we could see a picture of Mrksic as well. Could we see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At this time we will show the witness a photograph which has previously been marked as exhibit No. 26. This is also an excerpt from the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know if you see very clearly? Mr. Kojic, do you recognise this person? Certainly you did not see him yourself but do you recognise this individual? What do you see? Can you say what this means to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the name but I have not seen the person in life, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic, the Tribunal thanks you. We know it is not easy to come here to an International Tribunal. The hearing has been long; it recalls difficult and painful things to you and so it specifically would like to thank you and wishes you a safe journey back to your home. I believe that the usher can now accompany the witness out of the courtroom. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We return to the Prosecutor and give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness that we will be calling is Witness K. We are requesting for this witness some protective measures. We asked that his image be altered while he is testifying and also that the blinds be lowered as he enters the courtroom so that he is shielded from view by the public gallery. These are the only protective measures we are requesting for this witness. These were not previously requested in the motion that was submitted to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal, of course, agrees to grant this protection to the witness. Registrar, would you please indicate in the record the provisions that were taken to comply with the needs and the requests of these people? We are not hiding his identity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, just that his image be altered and the partition be placed behind the witness chair.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right. Would you mind having the shades drawn, please, so that this would protect the witness from having his image projected. Is everything ready, Mr. Marro? You might now bring the witness in. We are talking about Mr. Witness K. Witness K, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K, would you please take the headset and make sure that you hear? Do you hear me? Do you hear the interpretation? Do you hear me speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You hear me. You have a declaration which you can read before the Tribunal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K, can you please be seated, and please tell us who you are, how old you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Witness K. I am 26 years old.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We can turn to the Prosecutor for a second. This is a public hearing. We now raise the shades. Does Mr. Witness K know -- he does know that he has had his requests complied with. You can, therefore, testify with serenity before this Tribunal knowing that your identity has been protected, as you have requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K, which city are you from originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Have you lived in Zagreb most of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your nationality is Croatian, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You were living in Zagreb in the early part of the year 1991, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point in time did you enter into the Croatian National Guard, the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That occurred in August 1991, early August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did you come to join the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the situation in Croatia was such that Croatia was being attacked, I felt I needed to join the defences of my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you joined the National Guard, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the National Guards on 5th August 1991. Then we went to Kumrovec for training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did this training period last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very short, some 20 days, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left on 30th September, and I entered Vukovar early morning on 1st Of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Bogdanovci on buses, on a bus, and then we walked to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that point in time was Vukovar almost entirely cut off from the outside world by the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to go down a road to get into Vukovar? How did you actually get into the city itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a side road, we had a guide, local guide, who took us through the fields and so we entered the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many men did you go there with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit had about 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened after you arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were assigned to defend the Silos on the Danube River, and our duty was to protect the city against the crossings by the Yugoslav Army across the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What type of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had light, small arms, rifles, Kalashnikov rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What type of weapons were the JNA using that you were fighting against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything, all the full range that you can imagine an army would have in its arsenal -- aircraft, tanks, heavy guns, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you remain at this same position guarding the Silos throughout the whole course of the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did you change positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably around the 20th of October we left to take another position in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where did you go at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to a part of the city called Sajmiste by the local people, but the street name was Prvomajska Street, the "1st May Street".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: By the middle of November what was the overall situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we concluded and saw clearly that the city would fall. The situation was difficult, I must say. You could see that the army had already taken some parts of the city and pushing us towards the city centre, and we saw that the city was -- it was not possible to defend the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went to Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When exactly did this occur, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on 16th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the reason why you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my entire unit was wounded, so to speak, I was the only one that was not wounded at that time, and I felt that my best bet would be to wait in the hospital for the surrender of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the situation like when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, there were lots of wounded people, and there was fear in the air. It was obvious to everybody that the city would fall, and there was panic, people were panicky, fearing for what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there a lot of other people gathered there other than the wounded, civilians from other parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially -- not on the 16th, but then later when the city actually fell, then masses of people fled to the hospital, mostly civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you take your weapon with you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was left in the house, in the building, where our last post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see other Croatian soldiers with weapons at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, personally, I saw nobody. I saw nobody wearing any arms, no, not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: By the 19th of November had the fighting stopped in the area around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The fighting had stopped because the army had already surrounded the hospital, and on the 19th of November, as far as I can remember, there was no serious fighting on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On that day did you become aware of the presence of JNA soldiers at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did these first JNA soldiers behave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we entered the hospital on the 19th of November, they did not react at all. They were cool, so to speak. They just walked around the hospital. They walked around part of the hospital where I was. I did not move much in the hospital, but where I could see, they did not do anything at all on the 19th when they entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th of November, did the behaviour of the JNA soldiers change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that at one point we all had to go out of the building. Yes, of course, they started to classify us, to separate us, to search us. They started shouting abuse at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened to you personally at this time? Were you taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken with a group of people, taken out of the hospital building. We were then searched and they were -- and then we were taken on to buses waiting outside, outside the hospital grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who conducted these searches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did they appear to be looking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They might have thought that we had weapons, that was my guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that they had you board some buses; where were these buses parked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were parked on the other side of the hospital. I called it the rear part of the hospital, that is how I imagined, but I never entered the hospital through that rear entrance when I went to visit my wounded colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It was the side of the hospital that was opposite the Danube river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, that is what I thought, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Approximately, how many men were placed on each bus, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, buses were filled, all seats were taken, which would mean that each bus was carrying up to 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Approximately, how many buses were there? Approximately, how many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near the hospital, I could not quite see how many buses there were, but when we came to the Vukovar barracks, I could see that there were the total of six buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you were on the buses, was there anyone guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in my bus there were two soldiers guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These were regular JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how they presented themselves to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that you went to the Vukovar barracks. This was the barracks of the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did you observe when you arrived at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed that there were lots of troops there, Yugoslav Army troops, and that there were also there what we called "Chetniks", I would say paramilitary formations, that were also under the control of the JNA. That is what I noticed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you use the term "Chetnik", what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally think that they are the most extreme Serbs who are prepared to commit any crimes for their own national interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These people you have referred to as Chetniks and the other paramilitary soldiers, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they behaved in the way that I would call, sort of, a kind of band or banditry. They did not really look like a real army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How were they behaving at the barracks when you arrived there? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time it seemed that the army was able to control the events, but they came with a list of people, a list of names, and they called the names of people disembarking from the buses. There was a bus that was empty, and the names of people from our buses that were read, these people were taken to that extra bus and they were being beaten there. On our bus we had not at that time been beaten in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did any of these paramilitary soldiers or Chetniks get on your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to the door, but he did not enter the bus, he did not actually go into the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to hear these men saying anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were swearing at us, threatened that they would kill us. They said: "You are finished, there is no Croatia any more". That was the kind of abuse we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were they armed with any type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long, approximately, did the buses remain at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say not less than two hours, probably more. I cannot tell you precisely how long we stayed there. I did not even have my watch with me, so I could not follow the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When the buses did, in fact, leave, where did you go at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know where they were taking us. I only knew they were taking us out of the city. We went through the fields. Since I am from Zagreb, this was my first visit to Vukovar, I did not know much about, you know, the geography of Vukovar, but when we came to the hangers I heard that the location was called Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You had never been there before this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Which bus were you on in the group of buses that went to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the fifth bus, last but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did the buses do when they arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we stopped, all the buses stopped the engines, and then the people started to disembark. I would say we waited there for some 15 minutes before anybody came out of the bus, but then people started coming out of the buses and walking towards the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to see what was happening to the people getting off the buses in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that in front of the hangar there was a file, there were ranks consisting of Chetniks and JNA soldiers. They took away parts of the clothing, took away documents, money from the people, any gold objects which people might have had. They threw their clothes on to a pile. But, especially, what I noticed that as people passed through these two ranks they were being beaten very, very badly. I must say that they did not -- they made sure that we could not pass through these ranks very quickly. The tempo, the pace, was kept in such a way that everybody should be suddenly beaten while walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you got off the bus what happened to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I stopped in front of my bus which was parallel to the entrance to the hangar, and there were also JNA soldiers standing there who made sure we could not escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that point. But I can continue the story, if you like, and then you will see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be easier then. You see, at that point we were not beaten outside the hangar but, as we moved towards these two ranks of soldiers, a soldier, a young man my age, around 20, he asked me: "Where are you from?" I said: "I am from Zagreb". He said: "What are you doing here?" I shrugged my shoulders. I just said I did not know. He did not swear at me or anything and I noticed that, perhaps, I could establish some human contact with him. So I asked: "Where are you from? I said: "Can I ask you where you come from?" He said: "I am from Ruma", that is in Serbia. Then I said: "Look, listen, before the war I used to come to Ruma before the war. I had a friend with whom I had some dealings". He said: "But where did you come in Ruma precisely?" I said: "I cannot know precisely the name of the street, but it seems something like Partizansikh odreda Street, near the JNA hall". He said: "But this is my street in Ruma". He asked me for the name of my friend in Ruma. I gave the name. I said: "Miroslav, and I did not know the surname, but we called him Kemo". He said: "Oh, I know the man very well". So we walked towards the ranks, and I forgot to mention, I said: "Please try to save me, do something for me. Look what is happening here". He did not react. He did not do anything, so I continued walking towards the ranks of the beaters. They took my clothes, the upper part of my clothes, not everything, a jacket they took away. They took my documents, my family pictures, photos, money and my ring, also the rosary which I had around my neck, and they kept beating me as they were doing this. Then I entered the hangar, but in the hangar there were a number of people already and many were being beaten, because those that were beating us, they were beating us with large sticks, they had chains, also with rifle butts, and not to mention the fists and the kicking with their feet. So I went to the left side of the hangar towards the wall, and then again they started beating me, but at one point I heard behind my back somebody said: "Leave him alone, leave him alone, do not beat him". So somebody took my shoulder, turned me towards himself. I saw that this was the young soldier from Ruma who brought somebody to whom he referred as Captain. He said: "Comrad Captain, can we save this man? Can we take him out of here? I know him. I know him from before the war. We are friends, can we save him?" The Captain said: "All right, take him out of the hangar and watch him outside so that somebody does not kill him".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Before this happened approximately how long do you think you had been inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is again difficult to say, to reconstruct the time, not very long. I would say from the moment we entered through the ranks in the hangar itself, I would say it would be realistic to say I spent only about 10 minutes, but, honestly, I cannot say; it might have been more, it might have been less, I just do not know, but my guess is some 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: While you were inside the hangar you indicated that you saw other people already being beaten, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see anyone who appeared to have been seriously injured or killed as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I could not see much, I only saw the beatings, and the beatings were directed at me as well. Some people were falling to the floor. But when I entered the hangar for the second time after an hour or two hours, because I was about two hours outside, and then I saw people lying on the floor motionless.
