I did not touch their pulse to say whether they were alive or dead but many of them were lying motionless; some were sobbing, some were wailing in pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that you had been outside for approximately two hours. What had you been doing while you were outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was just standing there and was listening to what was happening inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the reason why you were taken back inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was said that they needed to make a list, to take our names. There were some seven people, some seven of us standing outside so they brought us back around 6 o'clock in the evening. It was getting dark, and we were told that they would take our names while we were in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did they, in fact, register down your names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they took my name, but they did not take the names of everybody in the group. They started making the list and then they stopped the taking of the register.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Inside the hangar approximately how many Chetniks, how many JNA soldiers, other paramilitary soldiers, were there inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only guess, probably not very correctly, but my conclusion was that there must have been around 100 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Approximately, how many Croatian men that had been taken out of the hospital that morning were located inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I am thinking logically, if the buses would have some 50 seats, with six buses you would have up to 300 people then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After your name was registered inside, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken out of the hangar, and we were waiting for a vehicle to come and get us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time did you have an opportunity to talk with this JNA soldier again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I cannot reconstruct the whole sequence, but I will sort of reconstruct the content of what we said. I asked him what is happening, what will be with us? He said that these people will probably all be killed, that he is trying to save my head and my life. And as we were leaving the hangar, he told me: "If anybody should ask you anything, you and I are old friends before the war. My name is Ilija, nickname 'Stuka'". Then he told me that he, that all these other people will be killed but that he was trying to save my life. He even gave me some money. I remember again at one point some 4 or 500 metres away I heard some machinery. I thought that was tanks and I said: "What was that noise? What do we hear there?" He said: "This is the graves being dug for those who will be killed here".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you eventually taken away from Ovcara in the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to a place called Modateks. That was a textile garments factory, a small garments factory, Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long were you held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one thing I forget to mention, I am sorry. We were first taken to Velepromet, but at Velepromet there was not room for us and, therefore, they decided to take us to Modateks. Then we stayed, our group stayed there. We came in the evening. We spent the night until around noon the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where did you go from Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back to Velepromet again because at Modateks the Chetniks arrived there, I recognised some of them as people from the Ovcara. So they started shouting at the guard at Modateks. They shouted and said: "Who brought them here? Why are these people here? We will kill them all and we will kill the person who brought them here", they said. So under this kind psychological pressure the guards decided to send us back to Velepromet. I also forget to mention that the person who came to Modateks said, when he threatened to kill us, he also boasted, he said: "I have been killing all night so I can continue killing and finish you off. This is no problem for me", he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until 22nd November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long were you held at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six months. I left, I was released on 22nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that time you were able to able to return to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an exchange, a major exchange, operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Other than the men who left in the van with you on the 20th of November, have you seen again any of the other men that were in the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question. Do you mean the van that took us on 22nd November, or what exactly did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No. On the 20th of November you left in a van with six or seven other people ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: -- on the 20th of November from Ovcara to go to Modateks. The people that had remained at the hangar at Ovcara, have you seen any of them again since that time alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, not my group? Exclusive of my group, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw anybody of the people who were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. Judge Odio Benito?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. (To the witness): I just would like to ask some clarification about those so-called Chetniks. Tell me, had they come from Belgrade, from Zagreb or from Vukovar, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only assume that they were from all over the place. I cannot tell you precisely where they came from. Some of them would say: "Yes, we are from Belgrade or from other parts of Serbia", but precisely where they came from, I cannot tell you; I would say from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: All of them were Serbs or there were Croats among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that they were all Serbs and I would say 99.9 per cent of them must have been Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K, you mentioned first that you went to the hospital on 16th November. You were not wounded, was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I was not wounded, not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Not in the hospital. Then when they started putting people in the buses, you mentioned that there was an extra bus where they took people to be beaten. I noted that. "The Chetniks called names of people to take to an extra bus". Why was this separation? Were they different from the others in any way? What do you think differentiated them from the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say it was not the Chetniks that called their names; it was a Yugoslav Army officer who came with a list. He separated them into an extra bus. This was happening in the Vukovar barracks and this was done by an army officer. I could not understand the criterion. I did not know why they were put on an extra bus, but then when they came to that extra bus they were beaten by the Chetniks and by the JNA soldiers, but I cannot tell you what the criterion of selection was, why they were taken to a separate bus, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So the beating was done by the Chetniks and by the regular soldiers of the Yugoslav Army -- not only by the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some regular soldiers also took part, some reservists perhaps and the Chetniks, they all beat people together, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: They also took their clothes and documents, as you said; was that also done by the people of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at Ovcara, exactly, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In all these happenings, did you notice any person particularly in command of what is happening, giving orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On two occasions I noticed this. This was the first time that I saw somebody who I now know is Major Sjivancanin. I did not know his name at that time. I knew that a Major was appointed to take over the hospital. I heard it in the hospital. Then I saw him in passing. I saw him shouting, waving his hands and arms. He was fairly tall, taller than I am, with moustache. Now when I think back and so on, I decided that that was Major Sjivancanin, that he was in command. But at that moment I did not quite know this. Later, at Ovcara, I also noticed higher ranking officer, a Yugoslav Army officer, who came there and he said that he was a Colonel, but I forgot his name. I cannot tell you precisely whether it was Colonel Ivanovic, Ivankovic or Jorvanovic, something like that, but he introduced himself as a Colonel, a high ranking officer in Ovcara. He came with a delegation and was also a fairly tall man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Of course, if you see the pictures you can recognise them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sjivancanin, I would recognise, yes. Actually, I realise that was him later when I saw his pictures. I said: "This is the same man who I saw in front of the hospital." The other Colonel, I think I could recognise him if I could see his picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was he present during the beatings or during the choice of the people to be put in an extra bus, in particular, or just did you see him at the hospital passing by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean that second Colonel, not Sjivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sjivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Sjivancanin only as I was leaving the hospital, and that might have been for a minute or two, not more than that. As I was leaving, he was on my right-hand side and I saw him waving, shouting, ordering soldiers and so on, and there were two persons in white uniforms, probably some hospital staff, I thought, or European monitors who were also dressed in white. I cannot tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But it was clear that he was in full command of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the impression and it was clear to me now that he must have been commanding. I mean, now when I left the camp, when I saw his pictures, I actually formed the conclusion that he was the one who was giving orders. You could see very well; he is a tall person, he was shouting, issuing loud orders and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just my last question: you said that you heard sounds and bulldozers working and asked this person who saved you what that was. He told you they were building graves. Did you pass by these graves or did you see them or just heard the noise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went by. I only heard the noise. It was already dark. When I was leaving Ovcara it was already dark already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he give you more details about these graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. He said, when he left me at Modateks, he said: "We must go on. We move on to Vinkovci, Osijek, to capture these cities", he said. He said: "You might have saved your life but I may not have saved mine because we must go now to attack Vinkovci and Osijek".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness K.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness K, in the hospital were there many of you who were in the same situation as you, that is, you were not wounded but went to the hospital really because it was a place, I believe you said that it was a safe place? Were there many of you in that same situation wearing some sort of a uniform which would show that you were not a wounded person, but somebody who was a combatant? Can you remember this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say this. The hospital was not very safe, no, it was not a very safe place during the war, but we heard that the surrender would take place there and that it was best for us to be all together and I was prepared to surrender. I did not want to go out as a soldier and raise my hands and say "I surrender." I thought it was best to surrender in a group. It was announced that there were would be a general surrender in the group -- in the hospital and I thought that was best for me to do that. Whether there were many such people like me, I do not know. I did not move much about the hospital. I only saw many, many people. In the part of the hospital where I was there were -- there might have been other soldiers who wanted to surrender, but they were mostly people from Vukovar whose names I did not know, of course. What happened with my uniform was that I took my uniform off, took off my uniform, because again I heard that we should leave our uniforms behind and that it will be easier to surrender. So that the soldiers who come will actually be able to control their paramilitary forces better, without too many men in uniforms around. So I left my uniform -- I was in civilian clothes -- and what happened to my uniform I do not know. There was a place where we had to dump it. I actually gave my uniform to a person who took it away and placed it somewhere else. The hospital staff did not want to have any weapons, any uniforms in the hospital because they thought that it was better for the protection of the wounded people and that was better for all of us together.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Witness K. Two clarifications, perhaps, I now turn to the Prosecutor, but we need the witness here. Do you make any connection between the Captain that the witness mentioned who had given out the order not to fight any more, that is, his Serbian friend, do you think that you could identify this person through the witness? I do not really understand very well the answer. There was a Colonel, there was the Major who was recognised by the witness. Do you see this connection between what he said? I would like you to answer for him; give us that clarification for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, other than Major Sjivancanin, we have not been able to positively identify any of the other individuals that he has referred to. We have made attempts to do so. The witness has viewed a number of videos and seen photographs, but he has not been able to provide either a complete name of these persons or to identify them in any of the videos or photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A second clarification: when the witness alludes to the bulldozers which my colleague also noted, in your investigation -- I am now talking about the geographical location -- were these the same mass graves to which the experts went?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We can only assume that they are, your Honour, based on the proximity to the hangar. To our knowledge, no other mass graves have been found in the area. The mass grave that is referenced in our indictment is located a little over a kilometre away from the hangar and, to our knowledge, no other grave sites have been discovered in the area, so we believe that it is one and the same.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): A last question, Mr. Witness K. Did you ever see this Serb who saved your life again? Do you have any connection with him? Have you maintained contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I never managed to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal thanks you, Mr. Witness K. Before you get up, we are going to take precautions. To conclude the protective measures, we will now once again lower the shades. The Tribunal wishes you a safe and peaceful journey back to your home. What do you do now, Mr. Witness K?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an Army officer of the Croatian Army now. I am still in the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the higher ranking Captain, between Captain and Major, between Captain and Major.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are sensitive to your having testified and wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you very much. The witness may be accompanied out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Prosecutor again, we are going to adjourn the hearing for 15 minutes and we will resume at 11.45. The hearing is now adjourned. (11.30 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, before you introduce the next witness, the Tribunal would like to know for its own organisation where we are with the witnesses. How many more do you plan to call? We are trying to organise the work, our work and the work of the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are five more witnesses to be called. I can indicate that the next witness, no protective measures will be sought in relation to that witness. Then there will be two witnesses in which orders have been made and protective measures will be sought. Then there will be two final witnesses where no orders are sought in relation to them. So it is a total of five witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right. The next witness has not asked for any protective measures, so I think we can bring him in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Dragutin Berghofer. MR. DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutin Berghofer, first, I would like to ask whether you hear me on the proper channel. Do you hear me? Are you hearing the interpretation? We are going to give you a solemn declaration which you are going to read to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please give us your name, your identity, what you do now and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 29th of October 1940 in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please be seated. The floor is yours, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you were born in Croatia, though I think that your name suggests German origins at some stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go to school? Did you go to school in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1945 I was in a camp in Valpovo and then in 1946 I was deported from that camp to Vukovar, and I have been living in Vukovar from that time until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your training, your employment that of a decorator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am also wall paper layer and a decorator. So both of these and I have my own workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that in Vukovar you had your own business; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you did your service in the army for a period of two years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 24th August 1991 when Vukovar was attacked, where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th August at 12 o'clock, rather at midnight and five minutes, my house which is 12 metres from the barrack fences, and that night at midnight and five minutes they started shooting from a tank, or rather from the anti-aircraft machine gun. So the shooting actually continued every 30 to 40 minutes and that lasted for about three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When this started to happen, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when my house was shelled and hit I was very much frightened. I could not understand that this could happen. So the following morning when I heard the voices, I took the courage to go out. I saw a neighbour who was also a Serb and I asked him: "Milan, who has been shooting at my house, and who has placed me before the Serbs so that you are now destroying my house?" He said: "I have no idea." So I took a scooter and drove some 800 metres towards the city where my business was, where my workshop was, and from that moment on I never came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to your business in the city where did you stay during the course of the attack on the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my business was in the city centre almost, and this is a hilly part. So there were cellars some 20 to 30 metres long and they were dug into that hill. So I spent the whole time of the war with other, with some other people, some 2,000 people who were in these shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your family with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of my daughters was with me, then my son-in-law and my unmarried wife. My wife was killed. My daughter was taken out of the house near the barracks on 15th September. I have never heard about her, anything about her. She actually left Vukovar two days before occupation. She left with a baby that she carried in her arms and her three-year old son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who took your daughter out of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What of your wife that you said was killed, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, Vukovar was being, was surrounded. You never knew from which side the grenades were coming, but we saw grenades coming from across the Danube from Backa Palanka in Vojvodina. The grenade fell through the door of my business, of my workshop, hit the wall and my wife was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you or any of the people with you armed during the course of your stay in the basements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not armed. I never had any weapons. The last time I saw a weapon was 30 years ago when I served my army in the JNA, my army duty. In the cellars I saw nobody with weapons. You must know that at that time we civilians could not obtain weapons very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there women as well as children in these basements as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my workshop, in my business, I had 40 women and some seven small children between two and three years old. Some 30 metres away from my workshop there were also large basements where I worked later as a civil defence worker, there were some 500 women and a few children. Just across the street was another large cellar with some 400 to 500 women and children. I would say that within the range of a 150 metres we had between 1,500 and 2,000 men, women, elderly people, elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were all these people fed during the period of the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received food from Djakovo while the road was open and some people actually, who never thought that such things would happen. I thought I could save my workshops, my own workshop, my daughter's workshop. We were local Vukovar people. We thought that nothing would happen to us. Later various shops were destroyed, and we gathered what was left, to save the food items and so on, and towards the end we had only flour and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from supplying the people with food in the vicinity around where your basement was, were you also supplying food to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions we took food to the hospital because, you know, animals were roaming the streets of the city; there was no electricity; there was no refrigeration and refrigerators of course could not work without electricity. So we had plenty of meat. Sometimes we took food to the hospital because they did not have flour, they did not have pasta and so on, so we did actually take food to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you obtain the water from for the people to drink that were in these cellars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Water we had from wells, but even these wells were then destroyed. I cannot tell you precisely when the list of wells was made. Actually people did come and made lists of wells. We drank water from a well which had not been used for more than 30 years but now was reactivated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided to attempt to escape from Vukovar or force your way out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, trying to break our way out, we did not really think we should do that. We had television, we had radios, transistor radios and so on, and we thought there would be a truce, peace would come back, we do not have to leave. We always consoled ourselves with the idea that we could stay on, but at the moment when we saw that things were going in a very bad way, on 17th Of November 1991 a group of people decided to flee. I would not call it a break-through because they were not armed, at least not sufficiently armed, for us to break through the ranks of the former Yugoslav Army. These were mainly civilians. I joined their ranks, I joined them, deciding also to flee with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Chamber the circumstances of what then happened during the course of this attempt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th Of November around 10.30 in the evening some 350 people, including myself -- and in fact I was one of the organisers, I knew Vukovar very well -- in the direction of Borisa Kidrica Street, we went past the cemetery, through the Sloga Stadium and when we came into the forest apparently one of our friends, Mika Holika, knew the paths, forest paths, because he was a hunter and he lived on the outskirts of the city. So I went to look for him and the column of people following me. I came to the last person and I said: "But you are not the last." I said: "There is another group, another group, because you were too fast, you are moving too fast." So I came back to look for this group. I found them at the Sloga Stadium entrance and I said: "Why can't you join us? Why don't you join us and catch up with our group?" But in that group there were some wounded people, some people could not walk very easily, a friend of mine sprained his ankle and so on, so they could not walk very fast. When we wanted to catch up with the first group we did not manage. We were left to ourselves and they started to shoot at us with mortars from the so-called railway bridge on the Vuka River. We wanted to cross the Vuka but we did not know which paths were not mined. One of my friends, Zoran Njovra -- Njovra, sorry, Zoran Njovra, and Jankovic said: "Now, don't go this way, there are mines there." However, two boys from Nasice did not listen to him. They hit the mine and they were both thrown into the river Vuka. Personally I became very frightened, not the fear of death; I would not have minded that, but I would not have liked to be lying and dying in the maize fields. So with a friend, Marko Mandic who was the plasterer in the hospital and his wife, also the man called Jankovic and a doctor whose name I do not remember now. So we returned to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the other people that continued on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened with them I only learned later when I was captured and in Sremska Mitrovica, I was beaten very badly at Mitrovica and then I was again saying, "Oh I might have better gone trying to find the way out." They said: "No, no, you are lucky that you did not try to do this because many of those groups were killed, captured slaughtered, slain", and out of the 350 people not more than 70, not more than 70 were saved, those people who tried to escape on 17th Of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that when were you trying to do the escape you were fired upon by mortars. The people attacking you, did you have any knowledge of who these people were that were attacking you when you were trying to make this escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew that they were the Chetniks and the former Yugoslav Army because some of our young people had already clashed with them at the barracks and at the Mitnica district, so we knew precisely who was attacking us and who was killing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you use the term "Chetnik", what is your understanding of that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that they are, that you were lucky if you were dealing with the Yugoslav Army because these people saved their lives, but if you had to deal with the Chetniks, then they had no chance of surviving. Until that time I did not know that. They were apparently present in the Second World War, but I saw them for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, what happened when you arrived back at the hospital? Can you tell us the sequence of events when you returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was raining, it was a kind of autumn slow rain. I came back to the hospital and you could hardly enter the hospital from all the numbers of civilians that were there, women, children and the wounded people, people who were separate groups, so to speak. So I sat through the night with the wife of my late friend who was killed at the beginning of atrocities so we are now talking about the 18th of November. In the hospital there were crowds of people. You could hardly move because people were standing in the way, so to speak. From the 18th until the 19th of November I spent the night in a small child's bed. The situation was very difficult. There was no food, but on the upper floor I found baby food, that is the baby powder preparation. They are for small babies when they are five or six months old, the children are. So this is baby food. I found two or three boxes of that and I ate that until the 19th . On the 19th of November around 4 o'clock in the afternoon, or maybe 3.30, the first reservists of the Yugoslav Army entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just prior to that time, had you seen any reservists or any paramilitaries or JNA at the hospital at any time prior to then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not prior to that, neither one nor the other or the third kind. The first time I saw them was on the 19th of November around half past three. These were reservists of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When these reservists arrived at the hospital, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember a man, a janitor or a porter, Bogdan Kuzmic who was having a quarrel on the bed with Stanko Dubnjak who was also in the hospital; he was probably wounded. Kuzmic asked him something and then he said: "But what could I have done? I could not have done anything", but that was all I could hear. So I hid in a room, in a doctor's room. There were also some nurses there, and there was another man called Perkovic. So we were in that room. We spent the night with the doctors until the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the reservists did you see any other military people, JNA or others there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that evening, but the following morning, early in the morning, I saw quite a number of young soldiers and somebody who was a commander which was an officer. He was obeyed by everybody. He was a tall man with a moustache, with an army cap Tito style. He had a flak jacket. So he was shouting, he said: "Doctor, what are we waiting for? We are at war. All those lightly wounded people and civilians, should go to the left side. Here is the side entrance." This was the Sapudl Street. That was the local name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want to take you back on a couple of points. The person that you originally came back to the hospital with back on 17th of November when you tried to escape from Vukovar, were you accompanied at that time by Dr. Mladen Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He saw me on the 18th of November and I had been great friends with him for some 15 years. So he actually took me to that doctor's room, doctor's office, where I could be with doctors and nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Milan Dr. Mladen Ivankovic have a son Goran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Ivankovic's son was Goran known as "Dzo" (that was his nickname) who came to greet his father, and they had not seen each other for some three to four months, I decided by the amount of kissing and hugging and so on. Goran Ivankovic said: "I told you to leave Vukovar and we will be burning the city with napalm bombs". He was wearing a helmet with a five-pointed star, but he also asked about his mother -- sorry, he asked about his grandmother and he was told that she was killed when a big bomb that we called a "pig" fell on to the hospital. He was sorry for her not to be alive, to take the Serbian cap and fight for Serbia. That is how I heard them sort of talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want to sort out a few things there. The son, Goran, was in the army with the Serbian forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He had been away fighting outside of the city prior to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that. I had never seen him, but judging by the way he greeted his father and the father greeted him, he must have been away for sometime, I would say three to four months, although actually he was a student at Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Mladen Ivankovic was the person who was your friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You started to tell us about the day when you first saw the JNA come to the hospital, it was in the morning of the 20th of November 1991, and you described there a man, a tall man with a beard, was giving orders and people were being divided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on the 20th . On the 19th of November the first army soldiers arrived. On the 20th was that high officer or that tall officer. I only learned later who he was but he was ordering, he was issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you later learn his name to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came after being released from Sremska Mitrovica I lost everything and for two years in '93 I think -- he said 63 -- the BBC showed pictures from Vukovar, and we saw that man who I saw in 1991. I knew that his name was Sjivancanin, that he was a Major because it was written, the name was written down there, and he was speaking in a kind of military fashion. He was -- and there was a representative of a peace organisation or a Red Cross representative from England was talking to him. He was showing that he was not allowed to go into the hospital. Then he pointed towards another bridge that we called the wooden bridge. It was not wooden any more; it was wooden before. We could see buses and I was in one of these buses on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was it that you got into the bus? Who told you to go there and how did you end up on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning on the 20th of November when that tall man with a moustache said, "Doctor, what are we waiting for? This is a war situation, all these lightly wounded and civilians should go to the left side", there were some 300 people, 320 people lined in two lines, because during that night many of the civilians had been taken away and we who were left turned towards Sapudl Street. We had to spread our legs. We had to take all metal objects out of our pockets. They did not take the money, they did not take our wallets or identification papers; only metal objects, if you had a small pocket knife, keys and things like that. As you were searched by the reservists, ordered by that gentleman who was issuing orders, so we were being searched and then boarding the buses. When the buses were filled and when there were no other people left, the buses started towards the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the barracks" you mean the JNA barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely, yes. This was the only barracks in Vukovar and, as I already said, it was close to my house, some 12 metres. I lived in my house 12 metres away from there. So we were brought to the barracks and as young soldiers were guarding us nobody could enter the buses, but some individual Chetniks -- this was like the Indians celebrating the capture of a white man, so they would be dancing the Indian dance around the person -- the Chetniks were dancing around the bus. One of the group, one group actually broke into a fire fighting box which is always there in the barracks. They took a few axe handles, pick axes, they also broke to have the handles and to beat us with them. They broke and then they, as I say, played their mad dance around the bus. A friend of mine, Duro Antunovic, when he saw me, he in fact had lived three houses further from my house and we were very good friends, especially with his parents, so when he saw me, he showed that he had a knife with which he would kill me and cut my throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He was with the Chetniks that were dancing around the bus, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was part of the Chetnik group outside. I also saw Darko Gradina. Then I also noticed that some people were taken out of the bus and I thought, well, they are lucky, they will be saved, but I had to change my opinion very soon because two minutes later they were thrown into the seventh bus, military bus, where they were beaten mercilessly with fists, feet, kicked with the feet, hit into the backside, and then I realised that their luck was not very much or very great. That bus then left in a direction that I did not know. It was a military bus. It turned towards Negoslavci, but I had no idea where it was taking them. After that there was another car, a small passenger car, a Yugo brand. There came people, the Chetniks shouting and screaming, and they followed the military bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you at any time when you were in the bus at the JNA barracks hit, physically hit, or beaten by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. In the barracks nobody beat me. They only threatened us. Some person, Goda, said: "What is it, Beli? There is no more football", and so on. They just shouted abuse at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any guards on your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a young soldier at the door and the door was closed, and nobody entered the bus as long as we were in the barracks, and in the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the young soldier part of the JNA or part of the Chetniks or you may not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The young soldier that was guarding us was a regular, a regular soldier, a JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What then happened after you had been at the barracks? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in the barracks, I cannot tell you precisely how long but some four hours. That is my guess. So they must have been deciding what to do with us. That is how I interpret this. Then we turned in the direction of Negoslavci. Nobody told us where we would end up. When we came close to Negoslavci, we turned left and we turned towards Ovcara. Ovcara, at Ovcara the buses stopped and we had to leave the buses one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened as you left the buses? What did you see? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When my turn came, my friend and I, the man who lived next door to my workshop, Goran Mugosa, known as "Kustro", he was about 22, 23 years old. I cannot remember precisely. So I came to him, all of us came to him, because he was there and then my turn came. He took my money, my wallet and he took everything that I had in my pockets, and since I was not the first one, I was 250th to be taken care of, so to speak, and there was already a pile of documents, money and various kinds of suitcases because some people had some baggage that they brought with them. I had nothing. I had no baggage personally. When you passed from that point on, you came between the ranks, two ranks, but it is difficult to describe, but try to believe me, you could see all the stars from the beating. You were being beaten on all sides with every instrument that you can imagine. I saw somebody asking: "Do you know him?" because I was working at Negoslavci, this is a Serbian village, and of course I was working for them. I turned that moment and I was badly, awfully badly hit into the -- on the right side of my head behind the ear, and blood started streaming down my face. This was done with a stick, with a walking stick. You know that the walking sticks are used for walking, and that I was hit with that. Then I was hit on the lower part of my body but I did not fall. I managed to go past that and run into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got into the hangar what did you see happening there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in the hangar, as far as I could see, while running, still running, I saw some of my, some of the people that I knew, my acquaintances, some of them much younger than I am, but we were good friends; my neighbour, Zeljko Begov, was there, Ante Podruzic, Zvonko Ilic, Stanko Bosovic and others. They were all young men who had been taken from the bus in the barracks. It was awful to look at them. They had swollen heads, blood streaming all over the place. You could not even recognise their faces because they were massacred while we were still on the buses or rather in the barracks. So I soon realised that they were the people who were put on that extra bus. I know some 20 people from that group and I remember their names. I have written them down, in fact, to remember their names. Zeljko Begov lived only five houses down the street from me. He fainted four times because he could not stand and he could not remain conscious. In the hangar, in that hall in Ovcara, there were four or five people who continued beating us without interruption. One of them had a chain and one had a pipe, a piece of metal pipe. We were not allowed to turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of the people that were actually beating you with the pipe and the chains, did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was a high official, a Serbian official, and one was called Milan Bulic, "Bulidza" was his nickname. He was a butcher in the hospital and he literally killed Damjan Samardzic and I was -- with a stick, painless stick, which was, in fact, the pickaxe handle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see this happening in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was before all of us because the door was still open, and later when we left he was all in blood. In the hall, in the hangar, one Montenegrin was looking for a young Frenchman. He said: "Is the Frenchman there?" He was a young man around 20. But I cannot describe the situation. This was a horrible situation. You cannot even show it in a movie what he did to that young man. Then there was another Meho who -- one Meho was beaten and one Meho who was a coach of the Ovcara football club, and his left arm was wounded, was injured, and yet with that injured arm or with the healthy arm he continued to beat the young man until he fainted and left -- gave no sign of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later on in the day, did something then happen with respect to you? Did someone come to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pausing. I forgot one more name, one of the leading beaters, Stevan Zoric. I learned later that his satellite, so to speak, were his sons, so he was beating us and his sons were beating us. For about an hour and a half, the torture lasted for about an hour and a half. Personally, I was not beaten that much. They hit me on two or three occasions. The worst that I got was when I was entering the barracks but then Goran Ivankovic came. He took me, Perkovic and Guncevic, and Stevan Zoric took out Emil Cakalic, and while Emil Cakalic was leaving the bus and went through the ranks of those who beat people, those Chetniks, he ran into the hangar where that high Serbian official said: "Oh, Mr. Inspector, you are here too". So that that other group started beating Mr. Cakalic as well. This was -- he was a sanitary inspector, the municipal sanitary inspector. Then came my liberation. Goran came and he took me out and some other people. There were several more people and it was getting dark. A car was coming with the lights on. So we were put on to a small van, Volkswagen van, a Polo. We were put on to that and took us to Velepromet but there was not room for us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping there for a moment. The man that separated you, was this Goran Ivankovic which was the son of Dr. Ivankovic that we spoke of earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right, this was Goran Ivankovic, the son of Dr. Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Goran Ivankovic was, in fact, with the paramilitary group that was participating in the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him beating anybody, but he was in the -- wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Did he say anything to you when he separated you out from the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me: "See, Beli, do you know who Zambata in this group?" I said: "Goran, they are all young people, people that I do not know and I do not know their names" because, apparently, Zambata was standing next to me, in fact. He was, in fact, the brother-in-law of my son-in-law and I did not want to betray him, so I pretended that I did not know the name. Then he said: "I would not kill him but I would break all his bones."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from that, did Goran Ivankovic say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember anything else. He took the three of us and put us on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said you were then taken in a small van to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they brought us to Velepromet but there was no room there and, therefore, they continued for a kilometre or two, maybe two kilometres, they had to drive around, or maybe even three kilometres. I was sitting in the back of the car. They took us to Modatex. Modatex is a knitting factory owned by a German built on the along the road to Petrovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Modatex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was dark evening when we arrived there. There were many women there sitting on the left side in a corner, and there were women from three or four buses, I think. When we -- when I came to Modatex I was recognised by Dorde Pavlovic who was a guard, who was on guard that evening when my house was first hit on 24th August. So he, in fact, was working as a bricklayer and building a house for my son-in-law. So when he saw me, in less than three minutes, a tall boy came, a man rather, some 30, 35 years old, his name was Dusko and he was a hardware shop assistant in the Velepromet. So, in the darkness under small light he said: "Who is Beli?" I said I was Beli. He looked at me and said: "That is you then. We will talk tomorrow morning". So that night or that evening nobody touched us. We had two guards. We slept on some tables. But around 4 o'clock in the morning, half past 4, more buses arrived and the women were taken on to these buses that then drove in the direction that we did not know. Some seven or eight of us who remained there were given some assignments. My assignment was to wash the big room, to wash the floor. It was raining. I had to bring water from outside accompanied by a guard. That soldier started shooting above my head from a pistol. It was so sudden I did not even have time to be afraid. A young soldier was on an APC vehicle with a machine gun. He also shot in the air and he said: "Do not worry", he said, one soldier said, "Do not worry, he is celebrating his family's patron saint". That was 21st November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Vukovar area in terms of months after this period, after you went to the Modatex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not very long. Let me say only that around half past 10 in the morning a young girl, aged 15, came. Her name was Sladana Korda. She was accompanied by two young soldiers and she pointed her finger at me. I was taken on the side, to the side of other prisoners. The two soldiers took my arms, left and right, and she thrust a big knife under my throat and asked me, how many Serbs I had killed; where are my weapons; where is my uniform? I honestly was not afraid as I was at Ovcara where my knees were weak, and I said: "Listen, young girl", because I was a good friend of her father, we played chess together, he was an educated man; he was the manager of the Medica Company; Damjan Korda was also a judge, so I said: "Who did you vote for at the last elections?" I said: "I voted for Ivica Racan", and I could have voted for HDZ, although I never was any member of any political organisation, only of football organisations, football clubs, like Dinamo in Zagreb. When she finished with her threats and attacks, then she took a cigarette from the young soldier, came to me two centimetres from my eye. She was going to extinguish the cigarette on my eyelids, but she did not do that. Then I was released. They left me, but around 1 o'clock, half past one, this was in the afternoon, Bulidza came -- the same Bulidza that beat and killed Damjan Samardzic at the Ovcara -- and he said: "Listen, Beli", he said, "you mother fuckers, who brought you here?" Perkovic and I said in one voice: "We are brought by Ivankovic, by Goran Ivankovic, Dzo". He had a nickname "Dzo". Then he said, and he would fuck the mother of him and us. He says: "I first kill him and then I will finish with you". We were guarded by a Serb who was a reservist with whom I was very good friends during the civilian times. He was known by the nickname of "Deda" and he treated us very nicely. When we arrived around 12 o'clock, we were given some bread and liver paste, so we shared this and ate. Then he locked us up. In an hour, an hour and a half, he unlocked that room and said: "I will take you to Velepromet; that is where military police is and where you will be safer than you are here". I remember that Zelimir Stankovic took us to Velepromet in the company of another soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At any of this stage or any of this time did you hear any discussion about what had happened to the people at Ovcara that were left behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard something, but since my right ear was badly damaged from the beating and there was blood in my ear I could not hear very well, but I heard him say, "I have killed quite a number of them tonight; I can do the same to you today." That was the tone of voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then when you were taken to Velepromet for the second time, taken back there, from where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they brought us to Velepromet. We were searched again but we had nothing in our pockets anyway. In the evening they took out some four to five people and these people I never saw again. They took Zerk Golac, then the son of a gypsy musician, and they took out a boy, a young man, who had been the one that was the witness to this court before me, so he was returned, and the rest of the people I never saw again. Among the people that were taken out was Perkovic, one who came with me from Ovcara. He was taken by Draca, the butcher's son. He was hit in the face with an army boot and he said: "I will first kill your -- cut your ear and then your throat; get out of here", they said. Around half past 10 two young soldiers arrived -- and let me add also when we entered, when we entered the hangar or, rather, when we entered the hut, and when the young soldier found nothing in my pockets, we had little money that we received from the doctor's son at Ovcara, so he asked: "What have you got in your shoes?" I had nothing in my shoes. "If I find anything in your shoes, I will cut your feet". I said: "You can cut them easily". Anyway, so four or five people were taken out, and around 11 o'clock in the evening, two more young soldiers walked into our room and said: "Do not be afraid, the Captain is trying to save you. Let us go and push the bus." So we came out. We pushed the bus that would not start. The engine started and they took us to the barracks. In the barracks each was given 20, 25 decogrammes of bread, a packet of cigarettes and a meat can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go then from the barracks until you were released, finally released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we spent the night in the barracks and in the morning a young soldier arrived, came in, and asked us for -- asked for our names, surnames, nationality. I said I was a Yugoslav, but he did not manage to get my name right, my surname right. "Berghofer" is difficult. So he actually gave me the name "Yugoslav". He called the names after an hour and he said those names that I read should come out, and he said the Yugoslav should also go. I was the last one. So we boarded the bus, and that took us direct to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From there what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now we are talking about 22nd November, and again at Mitrovica there was also, there were two ranks, two files of policemen lined up to the right and left, and we had to go between these two ranks and they used every opportunity to hit us, beat us with batons, kicked us. At that moment I was not kicked, I was only beaten. So we had to take all our clothes, we were naked. Then they continued to hit us. They used karate technique to hit us. One hit me on the stomach with a karate move. We had to lie down, lie on the floor and they continued to beat us. I was being badly beaten. I fainted on three occasions. At that time Soljic was killed. After two hours lying in the cold, he simply froze. So that this one slaughterer that hit me, in particular, that singled me out, his name was Dusko. One man called, told him, he said: "Dusko, how can you beat such a person? How can you beat him so badly?" I did not know what Dusko answered, but I know that he was laughing or sneering at the dead body. I know -- in fact, there were two dead bodies; one was the son of Kata Solic who froze to death, and he says: "Look at him, he has had too much ice cream". I was fainting repeatedly. I could not stand on my feet. So I fell, I collapsed, and one soldier allowed me to sit. Later Slobodan Nikolic and Buljan, Zeljko Buljan, took me, carried me, to a room 3 by 3 metres in size. I could not walk for five days. In fact, my skin was totally shrunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then on 27th March 1992 were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th, 27th, yes, at Nemetin I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From that time until now have you ever seen any of the people that were left behind at Ovcara at the time you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no nobody. I told you already that I have a list of twenty people that I remember that were with me. You cannot remember all the names, but I remember the names of my neighbours, my friends, but I never saw them again ever since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask the witness something. Were there always JNA barracks -- I am sorry -- I would like to know if were there always JNA barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there has always been one and, as long as I remember, there has been a barracks outside the city, a little outside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Barracks and soldiers? JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an operating barracks. It was always used with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the Chetniks, did they appear for the first time during these days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see, we used the name for -- the name "Chetnik" for people that were beating us, that were slaughtering us, that were killing us. But they all wore the Yugoslav army uniforms, and some of them had beards, they were uniformed and they all had the five pointed stars on their hats, on their caps. So it was difficult to distinguish between the Chetniks and the JNA. But some people from the JNA were good people, and saved some of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, if I can follow up the continuation of the movement of the events, you said that on 17th Of November there was an attempt to flee and 350 people went through the forest and, ultimately, only 70 of them were saved. Could you tell me what happened to the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening, I did not count them, but I can say this. I was the first one because, as I told you, I said when we -- if you go on the main street, you can hear the sounds of feet, voices and so on, it was dark, so I can say that some, the line was 450 metres long, the line of people. I also said that when I was looking for a guide, because we did not have a guide, we did not know all of these paths, but a group was left behind, so I came back to the Sloga stadium and the first group simply left us, so to speak, and some people made their own decisions. Some swam across the River Vuka. For instance, the brother of the late Perkovic who was with me at Ovcara, he survived but he was hit in the face by a shrapnel and two people behind him from Nasice, they were killed by mine. But I learned these things much later in Sremska Mitrovica from some people who managed to survive. So, how many were killed and what happened to individual groups, because, you see, the groups would be, would break up. These people did not quite know where they were going, and they were roaming in the maize fields. They had no orientation, depending on what happened to what individual or which group, much depended on how lucky you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned that some people were put into an extra bus and you discovered later that they were receiving a very severe treatment; you said there was blood and they became unrecognisable and their suffering was beyond imagination. Was there any reason for this distinction, in your opinion? Why did they choose these people, in particular, for a harsher treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, there may have been various reasons. First, they were young, young people. They might have had some personal quarrels with some people. There were Croats, Zeljko, Ante Podruzic. Then others said they could not live with us. I was 52 years old. I had no enemies in life. But suddenly somebody would say: "Yes, you are my enemy" and they do things to you. If your chicken walked in their garden, then, of course, they would say: "Now, that was the reason to do something". Not everybody was like that, and I would now say not everybody is like that, but there were people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who made this choice? Who made the choice of people to be put in this extra treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I have no idea. I was in my own bus. We could not come out. I could only watch what was happening, but we -- I could not even dream that that is what they were planning, to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also mentioned that someone came and was looking for a Frenchman and said: "I want to kill, to torture this Frenchman". Did I hear you right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you heard me right, but this was at Ovcara already, two or three metres away from me. The man came and was looking for a Frenchman and that I could see that. The Frenchman came with us on the bus and those who were standing by the wall, they came an hour and a half earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where this Frenchman came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him. He was about 19 or 20 years old. Maybe it was his nickname. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In all this what was the role of Sjivancanin whom you recognised? Did you see him often or saw what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Everything I saw was in the hospital. I saw him in the hospital when he said: "Doctor, what are we waiting for? It is wartime. All the lightly wounded patients and civilians should go to the left side". He was issuing orders. He ordered that we should be searched, that we should be placed on the buses, and many addressed him as a man in authority and I realised he was in authority and was commanding. Two years later I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the man whom you heard saying: "I have killed some and I would still kill again"? You said that you heard the man in Ovcara boasting that he has killed a lot and he is coming to kill again. Who was that? Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened in Modatex when Milan Bulic, known as "Bulidza", the hospital butcher, he came and, as far as I could understand him, he said: "I have killed plenty tonight and will kill you as well". Roughly, that is what he said; that was the main content of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal thanks the witness and is conscious of the difficulties which this type of hearing presents. You do hear me? Again, the Tribunal thanks you and is conscious of the difficulties which this represents for you, for the physical, emotional, psychological sufferings you have gone through, and wishes you calm and serenity. Our hearing has concluded. Thank you. The witness can be accompanied out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I turn to the Prosecutor now, and suggest that we adjourn this hearing and resume at 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned. (Luncheon Adjournment) (3.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The first question then for my side is whether the equipment is working. Mr. Prosecutor, can you hear what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is working here, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good. How about you, Registrar, and my colleagues, can you hear me? Legal assistants as well? Interpreters, do you hear yourselves? Good. Excellent. In that case the Prosecutor please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, at this stage I would like to make an application, if I may, to make a submission to you in camera. The submission that I wish to make will not take long; it is a very short matter and, for the people in the gallery who are watching, I would not think longer than about 15 minutes, if your Honours please, but for the purpose of this application, I would ask that it be in camera and I would ask that the broadcast of the proceedings cease for that purpose and that the courtroom be closed down for the application, if your Honours please. I will go into greater detail when I make my application, if that pleases the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At the request of the Prosecutor we will order an in camera session. Registrar, please could you ensure in technical terms that we can now hold an in camera session so that the Prosecutor can go into details regarding his request to the court? Yes, without a transcript, no transcription whatsoever. You can get this done in a few minutes, can you? Prosecutor, would you see any problem if this is taped, so this will be taped? Would there be any problem for you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all. If there is a transcript, in fact, we would encourage there be a transcript, your Honour. The only request we make it is not broadcast outside of the courtroom. That is the only thing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Recording, transcription, what you are asking for is that there be no broadcast to the public, so it is just an in camera session which you are asking, just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor. Very clear instructions there. We now give orders for the in camera session. Mr. Prosecutor, if you would like this in camera to be complete, we have to be clear about this. Quite clearly, we would have to switch off the video as well, would we not, the external video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Only the external video, your Honour. The videos that operate in the courtroom, there is no problem with that, but it is only that which would go to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Quite right, exactly. Fine. That is just what I meant. That is what I intended with my question. So please switch off the external video. Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor. Yes. Then there should be no interpreting for the public either, should there? Right. I would like to ask to the security services that all the staff in the public gallery should now empty the public gallery, in fact. The security services, would they do that, kindly? Registrar, would you pass on the message? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The floor is yours, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, we would now wish to proceed with the Rule 61 hearing. The next witness we would wish to call is witness B. He has been referred to as B and of which I understand your Honours have made some orders already. Your Honours, with witness B we are asking face distortion and voice distortion of this witness, and that he give his evidence behind the screen. But, other than that, the proceedings would be in public, your Honours. I should also add, your Honour, that reference to him in the course of the proceedings, if we could maintain the usage of the pseudonym "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, the order was already given by the Chamber. It has not been modified in any way, is that correct, Mr. Registrar? Therefore, I will ask that witness B now be called and will be called both by myself and the other judges as "witness B". I will ask that the witness now be brought into the room and once he is here, first, we can reopen the shades and then ask the technicians that the broadcast of the images be broadcast, in fact, to the public. Thank you, Registrar, for ensuring that everything is in the proper place.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that the usher has gone to get witness B. (Witness B was called)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness B, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are going to be given a declaration and asked to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. "Witness B", this is what we are going to call you throughout the hearing in accordance with some of the protective measures that were requested for you by the Prosecutor, and by you as well. All these measures of protection have now been taken having to do with your face and your identity. You can now, witness B, testify in complete serenity and with peace of mind. You are before an International Tribunal composed of judges who are seeking truth, all the truth, and now gives the Prosecutor the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had your whole family originally lived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You attended a school in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I went to school at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then after you left school what was your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in shipping, a company, international shipping, in a firm called Transjug-Rijeka, export/import.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then I think that you got married and you bought some land near the River Vuka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, I did get married and had a family, and I bought a house with the help of my parents and I simply built a new part near the house, new part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you still in the course of building this house when the war started in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a house that had been adapted for living and this new part of the building was to be for my future life there. Up until the beginning of the war, I was very intensely working to building this new part of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you prior to that do your military service, the usual military service, from 1984 to 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did military service for a year, slightly less than a year, and that was at Karlovac and then at Pivka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe to their Honours the environment in Vukovar, the way of life in Vukovar, prior to the commencement of hostilities in 1991 that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to describe everything that was going on, but when you try to describe the life of an ordinary man, they lived in a usual way, lots of problems; everyone was trying to either do his or her own work, and after this social changes that had occurred, there was a situation of a slight confusion and so many things were going on so very quickly. But these things were far away from us and nobody expected any kind of a war let alone the war that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a mixture of ethnic groups in living in and around Vukovar in the period leading up to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very much. That was known, Vukovar was known to be a very mixed area maybe the mostly mixed area in it this part of country probably more than 20 ethnic groups used to live there, and they had to live through whatever they had to live through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And apart from the usual day-to-day problems that people everybody where experienced did the ethnic groups get along more or less in a harmonious way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that they did. They used to live a normal way except from some small problems, I think that people lived in a normal way and there were no -- the ethnic, belonging to an ethnic group was not particularly important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this begin to change when you heard of an event where some Croatian Police Officers were killed in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I can only speak from my point of view. Yes, the tension was there, but people managed to overcome it. People even joked with that, with creating of a Serbia, that something like that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did the shells start falling on Vukovar, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for the night shooting that was coming from Borovo Naselje and Borovo Selo, the real shelling of Vukovar started somewhere in July at two occasions, at the beginning and maybe at the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were attempts made to organise evacuations of women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was done in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evacuation was made in various ways. The HDZ organised it, the municipality characters, the church organisation; many organisations tried to send the children away. We thought that it was simply sending children away or to the seaside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did your wife and children go away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the last convoy because I insisted upon it. They were put on that convoy, and they never came back, luckily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of the attack upon Vukovar, the siege of Vukovar, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was trying to exist, I was taking care of my life and the life of my parents. They were constantly between their house and my house. We were trying to repair the houses that were literally disappearing.
