The roof would be hit with several shells, and then we would go up on the roof when everything would calm down and then transfer bricks. We were simply trying to try to do whatever we could in order to survive, and waiting for everything to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then change and do something else subsequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my decision to do something else. I was called to the town hall of Vukovar where additional resistance was being organised because the fighting was going on, and I was included in the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your duties in relation to the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My basic duty was to be in charge of part of the fighting units for mining and trying to prevent the coming of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. How many men did you have in your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit, the members of the unit, was changing all the time but directly there were eight people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you uniformed? Did you wear a uniform of any sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not completely because at that time there were no uniforms. When I started to be in charge of this unit there was not enough equipment. I only had parts of a uniform from the old JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you have in your unit? What were the men armed with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as a unit or me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You personally, to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not really armed because we did not have weapons. As I was their commander, I only had the authority and I had the direct communication with our headquarters. From time to time people from my unit gave me some weapons to carry, some automatic rifle, or just a rifle, but that was from time to time. My soldiers had either the automatic guns or what they called Pap(?). You know, that was the weapons from the former JNA. We also had hand bombs, grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Through September and October of 1991 what were your forces doing, what was your group of men and the defence forces of Vukovar doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We desperately tried to stop further coming of the enemy and we were expecting help of the international community, so that everything would stop and they would find a normal, human way of putting an end to this needless conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the situation like during these months of September through October/November like in the town? Were there services such as electricity supplied to the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very problematic question. We did not have electricity. There were electricity cuts even in August. In September there was no electricity at all. Everything was improvised, trying to get some other sources of energy but, no, we did not have any direct electricity. In short, it was hell in which we had to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were the women and children during the period of the siege, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I saw it. I had the opportunity to go through some shelters from time to time and I saw how the children suffered. That was desperate, awful, to have to see that. These short contacts were so painful. They also had to suffer. Nobody could really help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone during this period try to escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. There must have been people who managed to escape, but I cannot really analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about your mother and father that you spoke of, did they stay on or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did stay, unfortunately. I tried to convince them to go away while they could still get out. I offered them my car so that they could go away but they decided to stay because I was there, my brother was there, everything they had was there, everything they had ever owned. So they did not want to stay. Later on the situation had changed, even they changed the way they thought. When the first convoy of -- when the wounded left, they thought they might leave but that was too late already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about your brother, did he stay on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he stayed on. He was also -- he also participated in the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On or about 16th Of November1991, what was the state of the conflict between the defenders of Vukovar and the people that were besieging it, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the end there was heavy fighting, up to the last man, literally speaking. These last days, we can say that the organised defence, organised resistance stopped. I was surprised by that. People continued individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the organised defence stopped -- what was the date that the organised defence stopped, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very difficult question to answer, because in such events you lose the feeling for time, but probably from the 17th -- 16th to 17th, probably the official defence resistance stopped then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say 16th and 17th, do you mean 16th/17th Of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The 16th to 17th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the organised defence of the city collapsed, what did you personally do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, when I found out that our headquarters was not where it used to be, that is that we were left alone, I came back to my unit and I explained to my people that it was over, there was no organised resistance, and I showed them to the way because they wanted to go through the so-called individual or breaking through in groups. I indicated them the way they should go, and I chose a person who was a local person who knew the ground, so that he would take them out. So we were to part and I came back home trying to find my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So when you say you showed them the way, you mean you showed them the way to escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, because I thought that they might go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you did not go with them when they went on this way that you had shown them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I told you I went to try to find my parents. I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. Did you eventually find your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found them in our cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then? Explain what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I stayed there, I changed my clothes, my mother had prepared warm clothes. She managed to put, to organise some heating. I do not know how she managed to do that. That night or the other night we heard that there was an evacuation that was being organised and that a meeting point was the hospital. As we lived relatively near the hospital, that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you hear about the fact that the evacuation was to take place from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was -- we heard it on mass media on the radio because we did have batteries so we could listen to the news on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So did you subsequently go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital there were many people there already. People were gathering in the hospital grounds between the main entrance and the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For some time I was there outside with my parents and I was watching what was going on, and then I parted with them to see my wounded friend and spent some hours with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What date, approximately, again if you can remember, was this that you were at the hospital? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very difficult question to answer. I still have the feeling that one day went by -- was it the 18th or the 19th ? I am not sure, not even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it was around about the 18th to the 19th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was either the 18th or the 19th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital did you see any of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Dr. Bosanac and many others that worked there as staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you meet with Dr. Jozo Tomic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Itzaro(?) Tomic is somebody I do not know. I cannot say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then after you had gone to the hospital when you had seen your friend there, what was the next thing that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, that day the so-called Yugoslavia or the reservists, the Yugoslav reservists, came on the hospital grounds. They surrounded the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these Serbian -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the forces that were our enemy; whether they were Serb, they had various kinds of uniform. The first party arrived. They had the insignia of the former JNA, ranking officers, and the soldiers that accompanied them were rather mixed. Apart from the regular soldiers, there are some non -- there were some non-regular forces as well, unregular in the physical appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did these soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers were put around the hospital and they, according to the Major who issued the orders, they did not allow in or out. One of his officers was a young lieutenant who was trying to say, calm everybody and saying all would be all right. I talked a bit to the civilians and then I went to the basement and I do not know what went on later on when in the hospital compound and outside the actual building of the -- the hospital building, because from then on I was in the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see the soldiers doing anything to the people that were assembled at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I have not seen anything doing to the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there many people gathered at the hospital at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few people. I cannot tell you the exact number. Maybe 100 people were in front of the building, and inside of the hospital there were many more people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people in front of the hospital, were they patients of the hospital or were they just assembled at the place in the same way as you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People in front of the hospital were civilians that were gathered there. They either came there because of a threat or because of their suffering. They went there to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You went down into the basement. Who was in the basement of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement of the hospital were many wounded people, many of them were from Igreb. It was really crowded with people. I can say that many defenders of the town were there and many civilians that were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in the hospital basement or did you go somewhere else that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I went to one of the floors of the hospital, because downstairs it was so crowded that it was impossible to find a small place where you could spend the night. I do not know whether I went to the first or the second floor. There were some medical staff there, and that is where I spent that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next morning, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning I came back to the basement of the hospital. I do not know what I expected really. Rumour had it, it might have been around 8 o'clock, rumour had it that everybody should go out. Somebody was shouting. I cannot say who was shouting, but what I heard was that all the Kudj should go out, whoever could walk should go out through the emergency ward door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you do not know who was shouting, was it a member of the hospital? Did you know whether or not it was a member of the Serbian group or was it a member of the hospital staff? Were you able to make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I really do not know who was shouting and who was saying that we should go out. It was -- the person was going through the corridor, and shouting, "Everybody out". I think those were the soldiers but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You followed this order and you went outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went outside what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all lined in a row and then separated and then searched. They were trying to see whether we had weapons, pistols, grenades, knives. They were searching us and then they sent us to the right, if you look towards the hospital building, towards the Gunduliceva street in the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you searched and were things taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only searched me but they did not take anything. After they searched us they sent us to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now when you say "they sent us to the buses", are you able at this stage to remember who "they" were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the soldiers that were from securing the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the buses, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the buses and everybody could choose the bus they want to go to. There were three, maybe more, buses, certainly not less, and everybody chose the bus he wanted to go on to and they sat on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got on the bus did you see were there any guards on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two soldiers. They were guards plus a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was any violence used at this stage against any of the people boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened once you got on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there for a short time. Then they shut the door of the bus. They started the engine and started towards the centre of the town as a convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go? Explain the route.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went through Gundeliceva Street, then the square, Marko Oreskovic, then the street Bozidara Adzije, then we went through the main square, through the street Dimitrija Tucovica, then we went through Smaj Jove Street and Kraseva and, finally, we went to the street called Sajmiste. After that we were taken to the barracks which is in that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the barracks", what barracks are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official barracks of the Vukovar garrison of the so-called former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these the only JNA barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, that was the only one, maybe they had some smaller bases somewhere, but this was the only barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did all the buses turn into the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a convoy. The convoy arrived and pulled up in a semi-circle in the middle part of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the people that were on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zeljko Jurela was there; somebody called by the nickname "Veliki", "Boiler," called Damjan; there was somebody else called Kemal. I can confirm they were on the same bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were inside the base did you see soldiers who were on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lots of people, they looked very mixed from simple soldiers up to various people who were dressed in a different way, various shoes, various types of clothing, one of them was Brolja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised, especially because he was the loudest one, Jakovljevic Radivoje, called "Frigider". He was threatening the person sitting next to me called Zeljko, which I mentioned. He was trying to put pressure on him, why did he kill his wife, but his wife actually had died from a shell of the JNA which put fire on a meat vehicle that had to, that had to leave the town with the children. At that -- during that shelling his wife had died and Jakovljevic was trying to say that the other person killed his own wife, and he was threatening him and Damjan that he would kill them and he was singing Chetnik songs. He was the loudest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say -- maybe an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime, two or three more buses had joined us. They came from the same side, the same that we came from, from the street called Sajmiste, and the convoy came and after some time the whole convoy went further on. We went to the street Sajmiste. Then we turned left towards going outside of Vukovar, and then they took us to the farm called Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you been to this place Ovcara before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, as a child, I remember that my father used to say: "In the spring we will go and collect flowers, catkins" and so on and sometimes I went to fishing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe Ovcara? What is it? Can you give us a very brief description of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you Ovcara is or was an agricultural estate, a farm, and it actually was for the livestock production, cattle raising, and there were various kinds of buildings there for their production, for their livestock raising. Also, there were a few buildings for the farm labourers. This is a very small place. You cannot even call it a village, but just a hamlet, but it has its own name and is probably listed in the list of inhabited villages as a village, but the main purpose was an agricultural estate or we call it agricultural economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it once a State owned collective farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was what we call the agricultural estate, Vupik. Vupik was a company and they had different kinds of production. They had livestock raising, cattle raising, pig raising and so on this, and this was Vupik, Vukovar was the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you arrived there what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived there the buses were lined one after the other, and the buses were then emptied one by one so that people disembarked the buses, and in front of the hangar they had to leave all their belongings, all their personal belongings, or maybe also things they had as souvenirs or Mementoes. Everything was piled up and then these objects were thrown and dumped on the pile. After that, they were searched again and they were robbed by the group of people. I call them a rabble, or they were a combination of soldiers and those brigands. Then they were told to go into the hangar and, as they entered, they were being beaten with sticks, iron bars, handles and they were thrown into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you refer to the word "soldiers" do you mean JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were assisted by other men who were not part of the JNA, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I was trying to say. They were a combination, so to speak, of all kind of people, both military and non-military in origin, as I would say. There was a mixed kind of company standing in front of the hangar and they were the people that waited for us and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go down through this cordon of men on either side who were beating people as they went in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Like everybody else, I went through that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you hit or beaten at all as you went through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten in several parts of my body, but especially badly on my head, at the back of my head, and I had a cut which was very bad and the bleeding was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you got inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were, as I say, we went through the cordon and then people came into the hangar. They sat down on the floor. There was some straw in the centre of the building, or they were leaning against the walls of the hangar. In groups, two or three people came, soldiers and non-soldiers, and they would come and question and maltreat people, beating them with truncheons, batons and especially with the weapons. They would hit them with the rifle butts, rifles, and I know a man Dado, Dado Vladimir Djukic, he was beaten with his own stick. He was -- he had, well, he could not move so he was on walking with the help of a stick, and then that was broken on him; he was beaten with that. So they went around; they asked people where they came from and those who were not from Vukovar they were especially badly beaten. They said: "What are you doing here? Why did you come?" and so on. In the meantime, there was a man who had a whistle who was in charge, so to speak. He was there supervising, you might say. He had no special rank or anything, so he was not anything special but he did have a whistle. So, he would sometimes whistle, and send these people out. They would come back again and there was this kind of beatings in waves. In the meantime, also they started making lists and a soldier was walking past us. He was a regular soldier. He had a flak jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "regular soldier", again you are referring to a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the JNA soldier who was dressed is in the regular army uniform, and he did have a flak jacket. So, he had the JNA uniform, but that was the combat uniform, the combat camouflage uniform. He came and took the names of everybody who was in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to name any of the people that you saw in the hangar hitting people, beating people, that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know the people who were being beaten, but I did not know those who were doing the beating. But in a video, later on a video recording, I saw a person and that was the person that maltreated people more than everybody else. I would say with -- I would say that that person also killed people, because I remember seeing him hitting a man called Kemal. That was a metre or two metres away from where I was standing. He actually killed him by beating him, assisted with -- assisted by his friends or comrades or fellow participants. So the man Kemal was actually trampled to death. He was kicked and while Kemal still showed some kinds of life, he asked him to sing about the Chetnik commander, a song about the Chetnik commander and so on. They had their own songs which they loved to hear, and after that Kemal showed no signs of life after all the trampling, and I am convinced that he was actually killed there on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there anyone else, in particular, who you knew, who you could name, whom you saw being beaten in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Dado Djukic, he was also very badly beaten and several other people were hit from all sides. I only know the name "Damjan", but I do not know his surname. He was our -- he was a driver in the hospital and he was driving wounded people. He was hit with a rifle butt and with the upper part of the rifle. That was a very bad beating; it was horrible to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: All in all, how long did you stay in this hangar for, approximately, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to say how long because the notion of time, I think, I totally lost track of time, but I know that it was getting dark and they had reflectors on us. This was actually almost winter, late autumn. So, after 5 o'clock it was getting dark. So, we probably spent some two to three hours there, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they started taking people out. They would take a few people out, some 20 people, maybe less, maybe fewer, so they would simply go there and they would take them through the door. This was happening at particular intervals, let us say, at the intervals of 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My turn came, my group was taken out, and we were told to go to another hangar. So they actually put us into a van, a military van, and they put us on to that van and closed the trampoline, so this was covered with a canvas and they transported us towards Grabovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Towards Grabovo. How big was this truck? Was it a very large truck or a small truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say smaller truck. It was a military truck, less than two tonnes capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many, approximately, men were in your group that were loaded on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say up to 20, not more than 20, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that the truck was covered with a canvas. How did you board the truck? What were the means of getting on or off it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the back part, in the rear part, of the truck, there was a ladder, a collapsible ladder, which was let down and after we boarded they lifted the ladder and actually you could not come out. The rest was covered with a canvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got into the back of the truck, were you only there with prisoners or was there a guard in the truck with you, in the back of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no guard. It was just us, the prisoners, we unfortunate people, but nobody from their part was in the back part of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago in your evidence that you drove off towards Grabovo. How far is Grabovo, approximately, from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe two kilometres, a little bit more -- not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you make it all the way to Grabovo or did something happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, half the way towards Grabovo there is a valley and in that valley the vehicle started to stop, to brake and the vehicle turned left towards a forest, a grove, on the left-hand, on the left side of that grove or forest. So we continued at a very slow speed. The vehicle did not stop but moved very slowly and -- yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the road like that goes along beside the forest? Is it a formed road or can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not really a road; this was a dirt track where you could actually drive. When forest work was done or when tractors had to go into the fields, this was the kind of path. This was not a normal road, but it was just a field or forest path.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the truck was travelling along that, what speed was it doing, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slow, maybe some 20 to 30 kilometres per hour, not more than that, because this was a rough kind of road and the speed could not be picked up at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This area where you were driving along, were you familiar with this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. I did not know that part of the surrounding area very well, but the other side, to the right of the valley, I knew very well, but I had never been to that left part of the valley. I only sort of remembered it driving along the road, that you could see the forest on the left-hand side but I never went in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were going along at this very slow speed along this dirt track, did you hear the men talking about something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a man in my group, his name is Mato Perak; he tried to -- he was thinking of escaping, of jumping off the truck, but Zeljko that I mentioned earlier stopped him and said: "Do not do that because we will all be killed if you escape." So he did not allow him to escape fearing for himself, so to speak. Then he did not just know what to do, should he escape, should he not escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point I decided that I would try to escape and I did. I jumped off the truck through this small opening in the back where the ladder is usually kept, and I jumped off the truck not knowing where I was and what I was doing really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you jumped off the truck, how did you land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I landed on my feet and legs and I made some kind of acrobatic jump, if you like, and I fell on my hand and feet. Immediately I got up and started to run towards, up the hill rather, to the left side in the direction of the movement of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you follow the vehicle, where it went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No interpretation). Very soon, very soon I came -- I am sorry -- I came to the middle of the hill and after that, from that point on I could not see the truck any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were running towards Vukovar or heading towards the other side of the field, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that time. I only heard the noise of the vehicle. There was some kind of monotonous noise of the vehicle moving along the path. Since it was night and very calm and quiet you could hear this noise for quite some time. Now I was starting to run behind the hill, on the other side of the hill. I heard that the vehicle stopped and at the same time I would say I heard a short burst of fire and several individual shots from several kinds of automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just for the clarification of record, do you mean gunfire from a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was rifle fire I think or machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I was running all the time, so I simply continued to run. Occasionally I would slow down and walk and then run again to come as fast, as far as possible, but I could not run all the time because I was getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going back to when you heard the rifle fire, did you hear a lot of fire or was it just a very short round of fire that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a short round of fire. I still have it in my ears. This was a short burst of fire, followed by several individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I came close to the city, to the place called Mitnica I tried to avoid that part, and I went through the maize fields and I came to Sajmiste where the barracks was. So I went past that. I saw another military building with a radar on it. Then I continued running towards Bogdanovci. I went through the Petrovos Road, came into the open fields again and continued towards Bogdanovci. My ultimate objective was to come to Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I managed to come to a place which I thought would be the village of Seric, and going through the village I decided that I was too close to the battle lines where perhaps mines had been laid and so on. Since I was very tired and exhausted, totally without water, I went back to try to look for some water, to find some water, and I went into a cellar. Then I woke the occupants, the military reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The cellar you went into was occupied, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was, the whole village was occupied. This was the village of Seric which was in the hands of the enemy army that we were trying to defend Vukovar from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think my question may have confused you. The cellar itself, were there people in the cellar that you went into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said earlier that there were soldiers in the cellar and I woke them up. They were the ones who were supposed to be on guard duty, but they were not and I surprised them. There were soldiers there, but I was there and what could I have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you woke the soldiers up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they first asked me who I was, where I was from and then I, since they also pointed their guns at me, I tried to -- I confused them a little and I said: "I am coming from Vinkovci and I cannot live there any more, I did not want to live". So they had the impression that I must have been a Serb or one of theirs, so that they did not touch me. Actually, they gave me a pillow and put me in a place for the smoking of smoked meat and then they said: "Stay there until the morning and then we will see." I tried to run away from that smoking, smoked meat chamber, but they realised that something was wrong. They kept a guard outside (this time he was awake), and then he shot a few bursts above my head or above that building and said that if I should try to escape once again he will shoot through the door and try to hit me. So I then decided it was no use trying, so I left, waited to see what my fate was going to be. In the morning they took me to their, I might say, commander or officer, and then I told him more or less who I was and where I was going. I said I was going towards Vinkovci and Zagreb and I said I was trying to join my family. They then transported me to another part of that village of Seric where their headquarters were, that was an ordinary house, and they left me there in front of a door or in the corridor or in the yard of that building. Then some soldiers came and maltreated me, asking me had I been slaughtering people and so on. So there was some maltreatment, beating. They broke my arkade. So this was bad enough. They also took my medallion that I had from my father that he gave me before I left which I managed to preserve in a pocket, they took it away from me and they were sort of pleased with that. They said that we were the Ustasha, that we were the killers, that we had slaughtered so many children, that they saw something like that on television. This is something I had no idea about of course, and as far as I know we never did anything of that kind. So after that they -- so after that a guard was placed with me on to a large army truck, and they took me to the village of Stari Jankovci where I was beaten again as usual by the military police, and I was kept in a cellar where I met several similar prisoners from the town of Vukovar. So they also questioned me there. They interrogated me for a while. I spent the night there, after which I was transported to Sid and then from Sid, again being maltreated and interrogated, but this was done within a single day, and I was brought to Sremska Mitrovica. After Sremska Mitrovica, again after interrogation and maltreatment, I was sent to the Military Court in Belgrade where they started a trial against me, charging me with various crimes. In the middle of the trial I was in fact exchanged. This was the last big exchange on 14th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. I turn to my colleagues. Do you have any questions you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you went to the hospital you found many defenders of Vukovar in the hospital in the basement. Was that right? Were they armed? Did they have any weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The defenders that were on the hospital ground could not have any weapons, because our forces have forbidden that. Whoever would enter the hospital grounds was not allowed to have any weapons with them. Everyone was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that in the barracks they were beating in waves and people being killed and hit very badly. When a man blew a whistle, did you recognise this man? Do you know by any chance who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that people were maltreated more or less individually depending on who they came across, but I do not know who that man was. I can partly describe him. I do not know him. He was a very stout person; I could even say fat. I think he wore a moustache. He was in a green uniform. These were the winter clothes on him, a winter uniform, but there were no insignia of rank. I cannot know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not remember somebody calling him by a certain name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far was the JNA involved in the operations in your opinion in all these situations? Were they very obvious or it was the other kind of people who were involved in these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially the soldiers were mostly securing the area and the others were, they were surrounding around the circle with their guns pointing towards the prisoners, but those who performed the beatings were not dressed in regular uniform. So we could say that it was mixed. There were the reservists. There was the army there but also the reservists as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the army saw what was happening and was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the army was there and they were acting as guards and they were observing whatever was going on. They brought us there and they held us there under guard, at gun point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You must be very tired. I will not ask you many questions. First, I would like to know whether you were united with your family and how do you live now? If you could give us a few indications about that, if I am not asking an indiscreet question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is my life force because I came back to life. I found my wife, my two children, so I have a family once again. I think I have profited from this war. At the moment I work for a firm that used to work in the Vukovar area, but also now I work in a programme for rehabilitation which includes working with computers. So I am part of that now and I live as best I can.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony and is sensitive to the fact that you came and the efforts that you have shown on its behalf. It wishes you also a peaceful return to your country, and that if you cannot forget what happened, at least you can find some peace again in your country. We will lower the shades so that your anonymity be protected all way to the end, and then we will return you to the Witness Protection Unit for your protection. Please do not move for a moment. In order your security to be absolutely ensured, we will take further measures. We will also adjourn until a quarter after five. Please remain where you are, and the Registrar will take care of all the measures needed to ensure your protection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The witness withdrew). (5.05 p.m.). (5.20 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting Counsel, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would call Witness A. We are requesting the same protective measures for this witness as were implemented for the last witness. These are the same as were contained in the previous order of the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Please show in Witness A then. We will try to complete this hearing of this witness today, with your agreement, and would start tomorrow at 9.30. Then there will be two outstanding witnesses, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good. Fine. If we start tomorrow morning at 9.30, then I think it should be possible to finish in good time. So we will finish this evening with Witness A. Witness A called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all your headphones. I would like to start by asking you whether you can hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your own language of course. If so, please start by reading out the solemn declaration which has been given to you as a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. At the request of the Prosecutor and at your own request -- yes, please adjust that screen -- you are covered by protection of your identity of your voice and also of your image. So appearing before the International Tribunal you can deliver your testimony with a fully calm mind and feel quite serene about the process. We are now winding up the screens, but you cannot be seen so your protection is fully assured, but this is a public hearing. Prosecuting Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness A, you are from Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are a Bosnian Muslim, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1990 you entered into the Yugoslav People's Army for your National Service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When exactly did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 15th December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you report to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported at the barracks in Belgrade, the barracks Marsala Tita.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Marsala Tita barracks, were you assigned to a particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned to Tito’s Guard and my unit was Special Infantry Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was your direct commander of the Special Infantry Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit or the head of it was Captain Radic Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the entire brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the whole brigade was General Milan Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a man named Veselin Sjivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he also an officer in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was at Avalo at the military police there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was a different barracks from the Marsala Tita barracks where you were based; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was also part of the Guards Brigade but it was at another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what Major Sjivancanin's function was within the Guards Brigade? Was he commander of a certain battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- I know he was in the military police. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade that you were in was made up of a mixture of people from all over Yugoslavia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This included at that time Croats, Slovenes, Albanians, Bosnians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in the unit there were no Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the summer of 1991 did you notice a difference in the way that the Croatian soldiers in the unit were being treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before we went through the battlefield the behaviour started to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the Croatian soldiers given as much responsibility as they had been given before that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the Croatian conscripts started failing to show up for their National Service or begin deserting from the JNA, those who were already serving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As these Croatian soldiers left, was anything done to replace them? Were other men brought in to replace the Croatians which had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on they filled in those places with Serbian voluntary soldiers -- volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these Serbian volunteers different in age from the other conscripts who were serving there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were older.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the average age of the conscripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conscripts were between 18 and 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How old were most of these reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to 30 years; let us say 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did their arrival in your barracks change the atmosphere there in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the discipline the same as it had been earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any of these reservists who came in refer to themselves as "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they ever talk about what was going on in Yugoslavia at the time and discuss any type of opinions that they had about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were interested only in a great Serbia, a greater Serbia. That was their objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your unit and in fact all of the Guards Brigade left Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before you left, was there any prior indication that something was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Croats were separated; they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told in advance where your unit was being deployed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you first find this out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tovarnik is in Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court the circumstances under which your unit was moved out of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. What time of the day did you leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left after midnight at 3 o'clock, 3 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told to take anything with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, full military gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you given to get ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five minutes, which was usual for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you observe as the Guards Brigade moved out of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many civilians. They were throwing flowers on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again this was close to 3 o'clock in the morning, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3, 5 o'clock when we left Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this point you still did not know where you were going, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you think it unusual that so many civilians were out on the street cheering you on and throwing flowers on your convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was unclear to me, but the reservists that were in the brigade, they were, they cheered back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they make any kind of signs or wave back to the crowd that was throwing the flowers at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were waving at the crowd and they were showing their sign, the Serbian sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you demonstrate the sign for the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Where exactly did your convoy go after it left Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoy went in the direction of Sid and we went out of the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From Sid did you cross into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went towards Croatia and when we arrived at Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see when you arrived in Tovarnik? What was going on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were houses that were burnt down; there were lots of soldiers, tanks, lots of military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Up until this point in time, had you known that there was fighting taking place anywhere in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did your unit stay in Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I know that they gave us anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From Tovarnik where did the convoy go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like as you travelled from Tovarnik to Negoslavci? What was going on along the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Along the road everything was destroyed and burnt down. There was spoRadic fighting and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Negoslavci what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Negoslavci we saw a lot of soldiers. The civilians waited for us, local civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you saw soldiers, were these all regular JNA soldiers or did you also see some paramilitary soldiers there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were lots of paramilitary there, lots of Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the transfer from Belgrade all the way to Negoslavci, had you seen either Colonel Mrksic or Major Sjivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see either of them in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did Colonel Mrksic do when you saw him in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lined us up there and he was issuing orders to other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he review the soldiers as you were lined up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for a very long time at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we went on foot towards a field. We were dug in and we had to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did any part of the Guards Brigade remain in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What parts were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The heavy weapons stayed at Negoslavci, the police, the security of our command. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the brigade headquarters were established there, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you spent the night in this field outside of Negoslavci, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night from the garrison we went towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to a certain area of Vukovar when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we came to a part of it called Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there fighting going on at Petrova Gora when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you provided accommodations in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far were you from the frontline where the fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was your unit commander, Captain Radic, during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he establish a headquarters in the same area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He established his headquarters in Nova Ulica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where exactly in Nova Ulica were his headquarters established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was in the house of Stanko whose surname I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What type of person was Stanko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a local man. He used to be a taxi driver before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He is someone you would describe as a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he call himself a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Captain Radic also establish his living quarters in the same house where his headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some point did your unit join in the fighting that was going on in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long was this after you had arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where exactly did you become involved in fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Nova Ulica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the paramilitary troops, these Chetniks, also involved in the fighting along with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they operating as a separate unit or were they integrated within your JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were together integrated, part of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any orders given prior to the attack as to how it was to be conducted from the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you what to do or give you instructions about how to conduct yourself as you went into battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was in command of your unit and of these paramilitary soldiers as you went into the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe for the court how this fighting occurred? What was going on when you got up to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the frontline there were barricades. During the first day we started with tanks. One tank was hit and he was destroyed. So we did not go further on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The way that your JNA unit conducted itself in the fighting on this first day, was that the way that you had been trained to fight during your training period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the same army, not the way we were trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your unit eventually able to overtake the Croatian barricades on Nova Ulica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Several days after this fighting was going on, did there come an occasion when General Adzic visited Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he do when he arrived in your unit's operational area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went around and inspected the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you involved in his visit in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I personally took him through the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was anyone else accompanying General Adzic as he went through the lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had his own security people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Major Sjivancanin also along with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really remember whether he was accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he also present with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they held a meeting at Stanko's house where there was Radic and Sjivancanin and Seselj and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From this time forward did your unit continue engaging in battles with the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of these attacks by the JNA on the Croatian positions, were they forced further and further back toward the Danube River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were withdrawing towards the centre of the town because they could not survive there because of all the forces that went towards them and the damage that was done to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion at one point when you went on a reconnaissance mission with a JNA lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where exactly did you go with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go with this lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went on a reconnaissance mission and during that reconnaissance mission the lieutenant was killed. I took him in front of our command. He was all in pieces. After that they sent me to the military academy, medical academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did they send you to the military medical institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they thought that I became crazy, that I could not be normal after what I did, what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was because you had retrieved his body and brought it back to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and my duty in the army when I was there was that I should not leave anyone personally, not an officer leave behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you behaved in the way that you had been trained to perform, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some point in time while you were in Vukovar did you start working more closely with Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your role with Captain Radic? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was his courier or messenger, things he could not send by telecom and such communication means I had to carry the messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of this position as Captain Radic's courier, did you see him more often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was with him on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you present for meetings that he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not the more important meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of your role as a courier for Captain Radic, did you also come in contact with Major Sjivancanin more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some point in time did you begin working as a courier directly for Major Sjivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In this role, though, were you transferred to Major Sjivancanin's unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did Sjivancanin maintain his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sjivancanin, I do not know exactly where his headquarters was, but I know that it was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever accompany Major Sjivancanin around the battle area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go with him when he visited the commander unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What would happen when he would visit these other officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would be issuing orders. He was the one that was supposed to give orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these other officers reporting to him on what was going on in their units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it appeared to you that Major Sjivancanin was in command of most of the operations that were going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody else could be that because he supervised everything and everything that was done had to be reported back to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the paramilitary soldiers, the Chetniks, did they also look up to Sjivancanin as a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The commander was one. There was a single command. He was ordering both the Chetniks and everything else and Sjivancanin was the main boss in the way I could understand. He was the main person responsible for the siege of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with a building which was located across the street and a little bit down from Stanko's house where Croatian soldiers were brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to them after they were brought to that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interrogated in Stanko's house and then taken to an old house and every trace of them was lost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw them being taken into this house alive, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see them being brought out alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see their bodies come out or you just never saw them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the last couple of weeks before the city of Vukovar fell, what were the conditions like for you and the other soldiers in your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not human conditions. We could not sleep. We were on the battle front day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During this time period did the fighting with the Croatian forces get more intense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the artillery was hitting and shelling the city at all times, and then we captured street by street. This was our tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the day that the JNA took the centre of the city of Vukovar from the Croatian forces, were you on the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to walk around the city centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you observe there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were lots of dead civilian bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did these people appear to have been persons that had died in battle from the shelling or had they been recently killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were those that were killed by shells, but there were also those that were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that same day did you see civilians being assembled for evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they being gathered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were being gathered at a particular point near the petrol station in the centre of the city, and then were taken to Velepromet or Unipromet. I do not know the name but think Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you participate in this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally ----

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the microphone just went out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is a microphone problem. My interpreters hear me. If so, could we perhaps proceed? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I will ask the question again. Did you participate in this evacuation of civilians from the petrol station to either Unipromet or Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you participate? What was your role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was driving a car and I took the civilians to Velepromet and I would leave them at Velepromet. So I made several rounds. I went on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These were civilians that you were taking, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these older people, young people? Can you describe what most of them were like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were elderly people and there were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you talk to these people at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to talk to them but it was impossible to talk to them because they were so scared and frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you finished helping with this transfer of people, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Nova Ulica, to our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You went back to the house where you were staying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During that night how were the JNA soldiers and the Chetniks who were in Vukovar, how were they behaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some kind of celebration, lots of shooting. I do not know how to explain this. They were very gay and merry and ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Early the next morning did you meet with Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next morning did you see Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The next morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our base and then we went towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You accompanied Captain Radic to the hospital from Stanko’house, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital, the hospital was filled with patients. The cellar was full. The basement was full. Everything was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go into the hospital itself with Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you also see Major Sjivancanin there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Sjivancanin talking with any of the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sjivancanin and Radic went together while I came only to the entrance of the building, but Sjivancanin and Radic then went further into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not accompany them into the hospital, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At some point on this morning did you see some of the wounded men being removed from the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the wounded people were taken out at the rear exit. I do not know whether they were wounded people. I would say patients. Some of them were being taken out through a rear exit or entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did these people appear to be under the guard of JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the whole building was under guard of the JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you remain inside the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay outside the building for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were outside the hospital, did you see what had happened to these men who had been brought out the back entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were being put on to lorries, trucks and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were at the hospital did you have an opportunity to speak with any other soldiers or Chetniks about what was happening to these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. According to what they said the idea was that everybody should have been killed because they did not deserve any better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the end of the day where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back to our building, to our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again this was the house on Nova Ulica where you were staying, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later that evening did you have occasion to go to Stanko's house again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
